topics.title: [haliax] Add Pallas-Triton tile-map ragged_dot kernels for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
On AMD Instinct GPUs, `ragged_dot(..., implementation="triton")` now runs a second family of Pallas-Triton grouped-GEMM kernels, called tile-map kernels. NVIDIA GPUs, TPU and megablox behave exactly as before. NVIDIA keeps the existing group-grid kernels and block sizes, including the Blackwell `block_n` of 256. Those kernels are unchanged in the diff. `_TILE_MAP_GPU_FAMILIES` lists the GPU families that use the tile-map kernels. Adding NVIDIA to it is a one-line change, for a follow-up once H100 and B200 have been measured.

These kernels use Pallas-Triton, which JAX 0.11 deprecates; Mosaic GPU, the replacement JAX suggests, does not support ROCm. #9859 ports the same kernels to Triton launched through `jax_triton.triton_call`, but jax-triton kernels hang multi-GPU training on ROCm today. On a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so when the 8 GPUs of one process launch together, all but one fail and the step stalls at the next collective (evidence in #9859). This PR lands the Pallas-Triton version so AMD runs can use the tile-map kernels now. #9859 replaces them once a jaxlib release fixes the race.

The existing kernels give every group a full grid over all row tiles and exit early on most of them. In the tile-map kernels, the forward and input-gradient (dlhs) kernels launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a tile map built on device from `group_sizes`, as in megablox's `make_group_metadata`. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. The weight gradient (drhs) uses one flat grid over all groups. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are zero-filled. The old kernels leave them unwritten. Block sizes come from a per-GPU-family table that was swept on MI350X. Two launch-order options are new: chiplet-aware program numbering (`num_xcds`) and grouped tile rows (`group_m`).

Per-call times on one MI350X, bf16, balanced groups. Each cell is TFLOP/s for the old kernels, then the new ones (job 453824). The June expert shapes are G=32, with w13 at K=N=2560 and w2 at K=1280, N=2560.

| Shape | M | fwd | dlhs | drhs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13 | 16384 | 94 → 594 | 88 → 635 | 378 → 483 |
| June w13 | 131072 | 587 → 730 | 556 → 808 | 428 → 585 |
| June w13 | 196608 | 525 → 735 | 511 → 818 | 429 → 579 |
| June w2 | 131072 | 560 → 668 | 541 → 765 | 403 → 586 |
| Mixtral-like w1, G=8, 4096x14336 | 16384 | 425 → 771 | 383 → 861 | 435 → 593 |
| Mixtral-like w1 | 65536 | 629 → 792 | 596 → 898 | 449 → 591 |

A dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs runs at about 730-960 TFLOP/s on this GPU. A sweep of `group_m` from 1 to 16 and `num_xcds` of 1 or 8 ran at both shape sets. Every setting beat the old kernels, and the chosen AMD entries are within 5% of the best setting sampled.

The full June model ran on 8x MI350X with EP8, `gpu_pallas_triton_flash` attention, memory fraction 0.90 and 20 steps. The table gives the median step over steps 2-19:

| Remat | Batch | Old kernels | New kernels | Peak memory (new) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| recompute_all | 64 | 2.149 s (122.0k tok/s) | 1.853 s (141.5k tok/s) | 158.4 GiB |
| recompute_all | 96 | 3.080 s (127.7k tok/s) | 2.696 s (145.9k tok/s) | 164.7 GiB |
| save_moe | 64 | 1.988 s (131.9k tok/s) | 1.832 s (143.1k tok/s) | 205.8 GiB |
| save_moe | 96 | 2.867 s (137.2k tok/s) | 2.672 s (147.2k tok/s) | 235.7 GiB |

Step-19 loss agrees with the old kernels within 1e-4. Earlier batch-96 runs on these kernels took 4.5-5.0 s per step, and one ran out of memory. Those runs reused XLA autotuning results from the per-fusion autotune cache, which JAX keeps inside `--compilation-cache-dir`. With that cache off (`JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`) or empty, batch 96 runs at 2.66-2.70 s and its throughput is above batch 64. The kernels were not the cause: per call they are 25-35% faster at batch 96's M=196608. With a warm autotune cache, save_moe at batch 64 took 4.95 s per step on the new kernels and 5.62 s on the old ones. With fresh autotuning it took 1.83 s and 1.99 s. Jobs: 453914, 453961 and 453944 (A/B), 453791 and 453823 (cache reproduction).

The per-call numbers and the block-size sweep came from `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which is in #9894. The edge-case tests (empty groups, unaligned boundaries, rows past the last group, partial tiles, every VJP layout) run for both families on a GPU. The tile-map family also runs them on CPU through the Pallas interpreter. Tests passed on MI350X (job 453882) and on the CPU interpreter (job 453881), and again after rebasing onto current main: all 72 on MI350X (job 458117), and on MI300X 42 passed with the 30 f32 cases skipped (job 458116). f32 cases skip on NVIDIA and on gfx942 (MI300X, MI325X), because Triton runs f32 dots in TF32 there. `test_accelerator_implementation_value_and_gradients_match_xla` now runs at highest matmul precision, as #9922 did for the custom VJP test: at default precision, XLA's autotuner on MI300X decides per process whether f32 dots run in xf32, and the test failed in 3 of 5 MI300X runs. With the change it passed 10 of 10 (job 458222).

Background and earlier measurements: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027367267

Part of #9812

topics.title: [iris] Renew worker credentials before expiry
topics.body:
Renew worker credentials one day before their 30-day expiry, including while workers are idle, and persist replacements across process restarts. Restrict renewal to authenticated workers and admins; expired credentials still require operator recovery. Controllers refresh provisioning credentials, and manual worker creation and restart obtain fresh tokens from the controller.

An expired worker token could remain unnoticed while the log client reused a cached Finelog endpoint. After a timeout invalidated that cache, controller endpoint discovery rejected the token and log batches were discarded even though tasks continued running. The October 9 audit found expired credentials on six CPU workers; targeted credential replacement and process restarts restored central logging without restarting their seven task containers.

Deploy the controller renewal RPC before the worker changes. Worker tokens remain shared identities without individual revocation; a stolen token can also renew itself.

[Incident diagnosis and recovery](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/691).

topics.title: [grug] Add a Pallas-Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_pallas_triton_flash`, an opt-in fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug has no fused kernel. Existing backends are unchanged.

These kernels use Pallas-Triton, which JAX 0.11 deprecates; Mosaic GPU, the replacement JAX suggests for Pallas, does not support ROCm. #9853 ports the same kernels to Triton launched through `jax_triton.triton_call`, 12-24% faster per layer on MI300X and MI350X, but jax-triton kernels hang multi-GPU training on ROCm today. On a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so when the 8 GPUs of one process launch together, all but one fail and the step stalls at the next collective (evidence and a standalone repro in #9853). This PR lands the Pallas-Triton version so AMD runs can use fused attention now. #9853 replaces it once AMD's jax fork, which builds the ROCm plugin, fixes the race.

The kernel reduces each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V. Under a mesh, batch and heads may be sharded; sequence and head_dim may not. The lower bounds are computed here and not with the FA4/CuTe helpers, which treat negative segment IDs as padding and would make the ROCm path import the CuTe backend.

One layer's forward plus backward at the June per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16), median of three interleaved rounds in one process, jax 0.11.1 (jobs 457836, 457837):

| Mask | GPU | reference | `gpu_pallas_triton_flash` |
|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | MI350X | 20.19 ms | 6.77 ms |
| causal | MI350X | 22.26 ms | 10.04 ms |
| window 2048 | MI300X | 31.17 ms | 12.04 ms |
| causal | MI300X | 32.32 ms | 17.28 ms |

The full June model at batch 64 on 8x MI350X goes from 2.426 s to 1.853 s per step (9.32% to 12.20% MFU) with jaxlib 0.11.0, peak memory falls from 184 to 158 GiB, and the loss matches the reference run (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027803714).

Value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI350X (job 458164) and in the Pallas interpreter on CPU (job 458155), which is the only way CI runs them. On MI300X the bf16 cases pass and the f32 cases skip (job 458163): Triton runs the kernels' default-precision f32 dots in TF32 on gfx942 and NVIDIA GPUs, about 2.7e-3 off the f32 reference.

Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other. Masks that carry FA4 precomputed bounds are rejected, which excludes the moe_hero_ep, moe_hero_fsdp and fast_track variants.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [grug] Run the June synthetic benchmark across Slurm nodes
topics.body:
`--gpus-per-node N` initializes jax.distributed from Slurm for one srun process per node that owns local GPUs 0 to N-1, and `--replica-axis` sets the Grug mesh's replica axis. Devices are ordered by process, so the inner mesh axes stay within a node and the flags choose which axis crosses nodes: on two 8-GPU nodes, `--expert-axis 8 --replica-axis 2` gives data parallelism across nodes, `--expert-axis 8` alone gives FSDP, and `--expert-axis 16` gives expert parallelism. Peak memory is now reported for the process's local devices only. Every process uses rank 0's default run id, because per-process timestamps can differ and would split one benchmark's logs and profiles across several ids.

The device ids are passed explicitly. Without them, JAX's Slurm detection gives each process only the GPU numbered by its local rank, and the AMD HPC Fund nodes set no CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for Levanter to split.

On two MI350X nodes at 8 sequences per GPU, data parallelism across nodes reaches 78% of one node's per-GPU throughput (2.023 s per step and 11.16% MFU, against 1.584 s and 14.26%). EP16 and FSDP across nodes reach 70%. Those runs used an earlier form of the flag that read CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. On this branch, a two-node run of the medium preset with `--gpus-per-node 8` builds the same 16-device mesh, and the one-node default path is unchanged.

Part of #9812.

topics.title: [inference] Adopt the qualified vLLM 0.30 GPU release
topics.body:
Adopt the published vLLM 0.30 GPU release with Torch 2.14.1+cu132 and CUDA 13.2.2/compiler 13.2.86. Both x86_64 and aarch64 use vLLM source commit `3a054c458ca8a32609ba2bc578c4d9b93eabb395` and the normal installer's architecture-specific dependency constraints. The pins are generated from [the released manifest](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/download/marin-vllm-gpu-20261012-3a054c458ca8/marin-vllm-gpu-manifest.json), SHA256 `e8a9e8e11781e0c1021783c5b559b9de4f82d0b90ca496de48b208d81baeeb82`.

[Official run 38314409260, attempt 2](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/actions/runs/38314409260) built both wheels, passed their physical H100 and GB200 gates, and published [the qualified pair](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261012-3a054c458ca8). Independent downloads match the run's wheel hashes, qualification records and GitHub asset digests. All Python model files and shared libraries match the [earlier staged 47b pair](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-staged-candidate-47b411d5785d) on both architectures. Version metadata and the optional Rust executable differ; equivalence of that executable is unproved. The normal Python serving and trainer paths leave it disabled.

The Snowball serving-mesh fix is merged in #9401. Retain the regression comparing logits from identical weights on the canonical training and serving meshes. Fresh normal-install HF-export parity passed all 64 representative cases with Levanter on 8 H100s and vLLM on 8 and 16 H100s. Maximum logged absolute probability differences from stored references were 0.056754, 0.064367 and 0.055632, respectively, within the unchanged 0.075 Levanter/0.125 vLLM bounds. Both vLLM configurations passed exact runtime placement/stage checks and exact same-rank token/logprob repeatability on a 15,025-token sentinel with fresh recomputes. Cross-rank variation is diagnostic. These application results cover the standalone Transformers 5.18.0 profile.

Earlier Snowball and Hero runs passed fresh training, checkpoint restoration and HF export on H100 and GB200 against the 47b wheels in MarinSkyRL's combined profile (Transformers 5.12.1). Hero/GB200's driver finished before a worker pod was deleted during shutdown; four queued worker retries were canceled. [MarinSkyRL #944](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/944) reconciles the exact released wheel pins at `cb2565d6`; all six current CI checks passed. Its explicit applicability assessment retains the original four-case evidence with its source/lock and sampling limits. New normal frozen combined installation and repeated Hero ShortConv/FP32-bias weight publication checks passed on H100 and GB200. The separate [native Snowball checkpoint failure](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400#issuecomment-6129427326) covers a different path from this HF-export parity gate.

The frozen MarinSkyRL training and serving package set retains Transformer Engine 2.20.2 and its other agreed native dependencies. The earlier Hero/GB200 comparison measured 56.37 seconds per native policy update for the refreshed [Torch 2.14.1 profile](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/c9def79c0ac7d043879c669722aab311532b3b03/uv.lock) versus 48.10 seconds for the shipping [Torch 2.13.0 profile](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/f85737fc366d1f077ce9216b179a2a98a0bf8d14/uv.lock), a 17.2% gap. Several dependencies differ between those profiles. That gap did not reproduce consistently as a TE-version effect. Follow-up Transformer Engine 2.19.0/2.20.2 repeats averaged 49.489/50.198 seconds over 18 warm updates per version, a descriptive 1.43% difference. Logical rank placement varied, and one process used a replacement allocation. The original cause and performance equivalence remain unproved. These measurements cover native policy updates; the [trainer handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/944) owns the combined lock and its qualification.

The reviewed source landed through [vLLM #92](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/92). Romain accepted its completed admin bypass as a one-time exception; no further bypass is authorized. [vLLM #93](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/93) later changed only the cache-cleanup schedule; it is outside this release. The prior main `903f1cc6fb7bed4897bcebdcaa83487e07624edc` is retained at `main-backup/20261012/pre-903f1cc6fb7b`.

Keep this draft for final consumer review. Romain owns the Marin/MSRL merges. Consumer rollback is GPU release `marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac`, source `01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e`. The [paired TPU refresh](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10023) remains parked with its separate environment, missing `vllm.distributed.aux_output_connector` module and unexecuted physical gate. The [release handoff](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10022#issuecomment-6093743002) records artifact identities, application results, trainer reconciliation and rollback; the old separate GPU activation/promotion commands are superseded.

topics.title: [levanter] Bound in-flight W&B metric host copies
topics.body:
Keep at most 8 device-to-host copies ahead of the value being read when converting a W&B payload. #9600 started a copy for every array leaf at once.

PJRT's GPU client finishes pending copies on a work queue (`pjrt_async_work_runner`) that starts a thread whenever queued work exceeds its idle threads and never stops one. A step's outputs become ready together, so prefetching a watch-step payload released thousands of copies at once and grew the queue by hundreds of threads in every process. The threads inherit the name `py_xla_callback` because their own name exceeds Linux's 15-character limit. On a one-rack restore of the hero run, each training process grew from 1 to about 1,700 `py_xla_callback` threads within 20 minutes, about 3,400 threads in total. Each blocking py-spy dump pauses every thread, so dumps took about 3.5x longer; #9998 makes Iris's periodic dumps non-blocking.

A single-node GB200 repro (4 processes, d768 MoE, watch every 10 steps) puts the growth at #9600: its parent and main with #9600 reverted keep 1 `py_xla_callback` thread per process, and #9600 has 318–424. With 2,000 scalars converted by `_convert_metrics_to_wandb_loggable` on one GPU:

| | `py_xla_callback` threads | conversion time |
|---|---|---|
| before #9600 | 1 | 60 ms |
| #9600 | 418 | 31 ms |
| this change | 2 | 33 ms |

topics.title: [iris] Follow re-registered serve endpoints from Evalchemy evals
topics.body:
Evalchemy children now reach their serve through a loopback relay that looks
the endpoint name up in the Iris registry, instead of a host:port resolved once
at launch. When Kueue preempts the serve and its retry registers on another
host, the old address refuses connections, hangs, or answers 404. The eval used
to retry that address until the group timed out: nine groups on cw-rno2a were
lost this way on 2026-10-09/10, some after 16-20 h.

The relay (iris.cluster.client.endpoint_relay) looks the name up every 30 s and
after each connection failure or 404. It aborts requests still waiting on a
replaced address and replays requests that have no response yet once the
endpoint is registered again (for up to 1 h, then 503). A response that has
started is never replayed; the relay drops the client connection so lm-eval's
own retries apply. Each relay thread keeps a pooled direct connection, so evals
keep the direct routing that #9480 chose over the hub proxy.

The fix sits in an Iris client module so any in-cluster client can use it. A
stable cluster-level address (a per-endpoint Kubernetes Service, or
controller-side forwarding) would cover every client without a helper process,
but it needs a controller deploy and work in each backend. The hub proxy
already follows re-registrations, and it is the path #9480 moved away from. The
relay ships in the job bundle and takes effect on the next eval launch.

While the Evalchemy job runs, the parent now reads the serve job states every
60 s. When one is terminal, it cancels the Evalchemy job and the record becomes
infra_failed with the serve job ID and state. A failed status read does not end
the eval. Before, the parent waited with no bound.

Tests drive the relay with real HTTP servers and a fake registry whose endpoint
moves mid-run. On a local in-process Iris cluster, the relay CLI in a client
task followed a serve job that was cancelled and replaced under the same
endpoint name; the request in flight during the gap waited about 4 s and was
answered by the replacement. Not yet run on CoreWeave: the registry lookup with
a task token (the local cluster has no auth) and starting the relay from
$IRIS_VENV inside a real Evalchemy child.

Fixes #10030

comments.body:

A coordinator task started a fake serve job that registered `/serve/smoke-relay-<id>`, then opened the relay through the Evalchemy child's `endpoint_relay()` helper, which launches `$IRIS_VENV/bin/python -m iris.cluster.client.endpoint_relay`. The relay's registry lookup used the task token. It then cancelled the serve, waited until the old address stopped answering, started a replacement under the same name, and sent a request through the relay.

02:24:03 relay: Endpoint moved: http://10.186.213.131:10241 -> None   (periodic refresh)
02:24:07 old address is down; request 2 sent

topics.title: [marin] Keep Kueue-gated serve tasks in the placement budget
topics.body:
Iris reports a Pending pod as BUILDING, including a pod that Kueue still holds at its admission gate (status message `SchedulingGated: ...`). The eval runner's endpoint wait in `marin.inference.iris` counted BUILDING as placed, so the 2,400 s startup budget ran while the serve job was still queued for GPUs. Eight eval groups failed this way in one night with no GPU allocated.

A BUILDING task whose status message starts with `SchedulingGated` now counts as queued. The 4 h placement budget covers gated time, and the startup budget starts only once the gate is lifted. A preemption requeue still resets the startup budget. The wait now reads per-task status with `list_tasks` because the job-level state counts do not carry the status message.

A pod that Kueue has admitted but the scheduler reports `Unschedulable` still counts as placed, so the startup budget bounds an admitted pod that does not start. `Unschedulable` can mean a bad resource request or ordinary capacity or affinity limits; this keeps the existing behavior for both.

Separate from #10030 / #10033.

Fixes #10036

topics.title: [inference] Start serve readiness timeout after placement
topics.body:
Start the serve readiness timeout when a task's current attempt has an assigned Iris worker or a node-bound Kubernetes pod, or when the task is running. Kubernetes reports Kueue-gated Pending pods as BUILDING; the previous state-count check treated them as placed and failed evaluations after 2,400 seconds without allocating a GPU. Federated task status can also show a peer display label as its worker ID before placement, so the waiter uses the current attempt's assignment.

Queued time remains subject to the four-hour placement deadline. Requeued attempts stop consuming the startup budget, and old attempts' placement details do not mark the new attempt as placed.

Fixes #10036

topics.title: [experiment] BFCL multi-harness DPO recovery: results and remaining work
topics.body:
## TL;DR

The BFCL multi-harness recovery campaign did not reach its goal. We exercised DPO (direct preference optimization) in Levanter, implemented and tested native DPO in MarinSkyRL, and built trace retention, preference curation, and multi-harness collection infrastructure. The extended native DPO run degraded Pi accuracy from 34/123 at initialization to 10/123 after four updates and 0/123 after eight; we stopped it after preserving intermediate evaluations. Harness transfer was partial and large score differences persisted across harnesses. A separate model-merging campaign recovered substantially more measured BFCL-Parity performance than the DPO recipes tested here, with important selection and comparability limits.

## Description

The original objective was to improve function calling from the Grug-67B-A2B Antidoom/RLVR1 step-12 lineage and demonstrate multi-harness robustness: the worst harness should reach at least 70% of the best harness's score. Grug is a mixture-of-experts model with approximately 67 billion total and 2 billion active parameters; Antidoom/RLVR1 identifies its prior de-looping and reinforcement-learning checkpoint lineage. Labels such as `.304` and `.356` are campaign run/artifact identifiers. Training used the 3,518-task BFCL complement, excluding the 123 BFCL-Parity tasks. Offline DPO was used to improve the weak starting policy before attempting further online RL.

BFCL-Parity is Harbor's `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation of the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard. Pi, Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, and Mini-SWE are agent harnesses that provide prompts, tool interfaces, and execution loops around the model. Each evaluation task receives one agent trial; accuracy means passing the task verifier. These tasks require `/app/result.json`, whose existence alone is insufficient for success. The scores below are adaptation-specific solve rates, not standard BFCL leaderboard scores. See the [public evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9566).

## Hypothesis or Goal

Learn function-calling behavior that transfers across harnesses while preserving task accuracy. The campaign tested whole-trajectory preference training, not the localized token/action objectives proposed in the follow-ups.

## Status

Learning work is stopped. The campaign achieved these infrastructure milestones:

- Levanter DPO produced the `.304` initializer after two additional optimizer updates and a 39-shard HF-format export. This checkpoint descended from an earlier 58-update DPO warm start; it was not trained directly from the original model in two updates. [Export receipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/trials/daytona-expanded-training-v304-verified.json).
- Native DPO was [merged into MarinSkyRL in #954](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/954). Pipeline smoke `.356` connected fresh collection, curation, four applied updates, Pi evaluation, and export. Its 64-pair batch contained one newly collected pair; this was not an all-harness fresh-data smoke. Accuracy fell from 28/123 to 7/123. [Optimizer and pipeline receipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/trials/final-pipeline-v356-verified.json).
- The collection/curation path retains teacher/student traces, exact tokens and masks where captured, verifier outcomes, task identities, immutable partial batches, and preference provenance. Four harnesses supplied the final training cohort; Pi was the evaluation harness. These components support future datakit mining, but do not yet implement verified same-history local repair pairs. [Infrastructure inventory](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/technical-progress-20261011.md), [pinned campaign code](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl).
- A complete online multi-harness RL optimizer loop was not demonstrated. Collection, native trace capture, rollout configuration, and training components exist; their full on-policy integration remains unverified. Some fixes remain on campaign branches or open PRs.

The final native DPO input contained 1,712 pairs from 633 tasks unseen by the initializer's recorded training lineage. We planned 107 updates at 16 pairs/update, with Pi validation before training and every four updates. Applied updates are verified through 35, with nine completed evaluation panels and a partial update-36 panel. The initializer remained the best evaluated checkpoint. [Collapse analysis](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-collapse-investigation-20261011.md), [archive/stop receipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/trials/final-dpo-forensics-stop-verified.json).

## Results and limits

Levanter's short `.304` continuation improved the measured panel relative to its `.26` warm start: Pi 23/122 to 35/123, Claude Code 15/123 to 29/123, OpenCode 8/123 to 24/123, and Mini-SWE 8/123 to 16/123. The Pi baseline attempted 123 tasks with one infrastructure-ungraded result. These are single panel comparisons, not repeated statistical estimates. Public warm-start receipts: [Pi](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-pi-verified.json), [Claude Code](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-claude-code-verified.json), [OpenCode](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-opencode-verified.json), [Mini-SWE](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/7c63db4501ba6d3a523db18726d3855cf96b0afb/trials/daytona-reference-parity-v311-2026.10.04.26-mini-swe-agent-verified.json).

The earlier `.304` panel scored Pi 35/123 (28.46%), Claude Code 29/123 (23.58%), OpenCode 24/123 (19.51%), and Mini-SWE 16/123 (13.01%). Codex covered only 105/123 tasks and was not a valid canonical panel. The worst valid score was 46% of the best, below the required 70%. These results show harness-dependent performance; they do not isolate a causal training-mixture effect. The later 34/123 native-run baseline is a separate evaluation of the initializer.

The best related published merge, [Shared100](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-NUPA-BFCL-Shared100-2026.10.09/tree/462ad9af071055da39ef4bfea1d4ba2c9429a223), scored 60/123 (48.78%) on BFCL-Parity Pi, versus `.304`'s 35/123. In our experiments, merging recovered more measured performance than the tested DPO recipes. However, BFCL-Parity activation traces informed expert selection in the merge campaign, and the benchmark was reused for model selection. Its score is an optimization result, not a clean held-out or controlled causal comparison with DPO. Parent mixtures and training histories differ, and the merge's Pi score does not establish multi-harness robustness. [Merge campaign](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975).

At native DPO update 8, all 123 tasks lacked the required result file. Successful file-writing demonstrations existed in the preference data. Rejected responses contributed about 7.24 times as many supervised tokens as chosen responses, with extreme tool-syntax repetition. These observations motivate local, bounded training targets. They do not establish the precise gradient mechanism behind the collapse. Independent distributed-update and training-to-serving numerical equivalence remain [deferred verification experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/issues/969), not discovered bugs.

## Links

Datakit is [Marin's data preparation and chat-rendering library](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit). Linked historical reports retain local/internal provenance paths; the public release supports aggregate inspection rather than complete independent replay. Evaluation runtime pins also differ between the DPO and merge campaigns, so their results are separate campaign measurements.

- [Public screened campaign artifacts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/tree/9be5d36578c27140a75caac1e31ecdefb76cff0b): 7,356 files, reports, scripts, configurations, aggregate receipts, model publication verification, and an exclusion manifest. Raw conversations, private DPO datasets, third-party payloads, secrets, and runtime directories are withheld. Public aggregates do not permit independent replay of every private-trace analysis.
- [Best DPO initializer, BFCL-Recovery (`.304`)](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery/tree/850a32627724d274004241dd10f6cb46fd3f6f83): public, 39 BF16 shards, with all uploaded file hashes verified. The model card explains the inherited stale manifest and the scope of provenance checks. It received no updates from the degrading extended run. [Best related published merge and limitations](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-NUPA-BFCL-Shared100-2026.10.09/tree/462ad9af071055da39ef4bfea1d4ba2c9429a223) is a separate model.
- [Pinned MarinSkyRL runtime](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/fa6da4d8c67ed17b3fa69f689d9b444694683f8a), [pinned Harbor runtime](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/tree/436d0c92ed2fbb679438cd750e5fab3328153c31).
- Open follow-ups: [localized online feedback #10043](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043), [datakit single-turn comparison mining and DPO validation #10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042), and [complete online multi-harness RL integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041).

## Decision Log

- Used offline preference learning while baseline task success remained low.
- Moved from Levanter to native MarinSkyRL DPO to exercise the unified trainer and periodic Pi evaluation.
- Stopped the extended run after degradation, preserving intermediate traces for analysis.
- Separated future behavioral interventions from the uncompleted online integration work.

## Conclusion

The performance and harness-robustness objectives remain unmet. The campaign leaves tested DPO plumbing and reusable collection/curation components, with three explicit follow-ups. Closing this issue archives the campaign; it does not certify successful recovery or complete online multi-harness RL.

topics.title: Validate localized online feedback for tool-use failures
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Final-token preference optimization (FTPO) reduced repeated tool-call opening markers from 72/156 to 1/156 on a frozen-prefix diagnostic, a 98.6% reduction. Valid first-call syntax increased from 21/156 to 42/156. The selected checkpoint improved standalone BFCL-Parity/Pi from 30/123 to 43/123, while IFBench Loose declined from 82/300 to 78/300. These are single-sample validation results; capability preservation remains unproven.

The campaign is complete. The [selected checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Protocol-FTPO/tree/d761ea0a94500c2aa24aa4cd71b5a149d962e5c8) is public. The [exact benchmark](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Tool-Protocol-Replay-v1) remains private pending clarification of redistribution rights for captured client-supplied instructions and tool descriptions. An inaccessible link for an unauthenticated reader is expected. This precaution is not a finding that the captured text is confidential or that its capture violated any terms.

## Description and hypothesis

BFCL is the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard. BFCL-Parity is this campaign's fixed 123-task panel, audited against the full task set by the [partition code](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/data.py); its task identities are in the private benchmark manifest. Pi is the agent harness that executes model tool calls. Harbor manages task/agent integration, and Daytona supplies task containers. DPO means direct preference optimization; SFT means supervised fine-tuning.

The preceding BFCL campaign's extended DPO run degraded Pi task success from 34/123 to 0/123 after eight updates. That observation motivated testing a much narrower training signal. This experiment asks whether changing a preference at one observed invalid token boundary can reduce a recurring tool-protocol error while retaining task capability. It does not establish the cause of the earlier DPO collapse. Related work: [BFCL closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040), [localized feedback proposal #9691](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691), and [FTPO implementation #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887).

The implemented target is a second `<tool_call>` immediately after an already-opened call, allowing intervening JSON whitespace. The experiment narrowed the original closure proposal to this repeated-opener case. General closing-token repairs, short repair spans, off-top-K verified alternatives, masked-SFT comparisons, and cross-harness transfer remain follow-up work.

## Benchmark design and construction

The source BFCL revision is `6bedd7878dc5d6f3456b4d80b781eb3c2d84f262`. Its campaign partition has 3,518 training-approved task identities and a separate 123-task BFCL-Parity panel. Before failure selection, task IDs were sorted by SHA-256 of `repeated-opener-v1:<task_id>`; the first 704 were reserved for diagnostics and the other 2,814 for this intervention's training.

The builder scanned 717 of 718 retained trajectory archives and examined 5,771 records on reserved tasks. One archive was excluded for disagreement between literal opener strings and special-token positions. It excluded 857 candidate prefix occurrences over the 24,576-token limit, then selected the lexicographically smallest eligible prefix hash per task. This produced 156 unique task prefixes of 10,101–24,558 tokens. A separate training partition supplied 581 replay prefixes. No diagnostic or parity task entered this FTPO training set.

Training selection used the same source-archive set and repeated-opener extraction rule, restricted to training task IDs. It examined 22,003 training records, found 14,761 within-budget candidate occurrences, and excluded 2,880 oversized occurrences and two audited token-alignment failures. Selection kept the smallest prefix hash per task, then removed nine selected prefixes that failed the runtime boundary-selector check. The final 581 prefixes represent 581 distinct tasks. Archive overlap is expected; task identities are disjoint. See [training construction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6/experiments/post_training/skill_acquisition/training_data.py).

Each diagnostic retains exact model-input token IDs through an initial opener, immediately before a historical repeated opener at the first malformed call in an assistant span outside thinking. Historical source identity: `users/benfeuer/inputs/bfcl-rl-recovered-policy@2026.10.04.26:479563dc`. The selected prefixes contain its prior conversation and harness context. New continuations are generated from the evaluated policy. The source model is distinct from the later Recovery initializer.

The case-file SHA-256 is `9249b4a7f25d45ab6884c152cd6d975d71312e0c8ba1ecf29bf0cffaea62d8ed`. The Recovery tokenizer SHA-256 is `6a61ca2105a54e9984169b409581f31cc50330d1b47104af13c221b05e462e45`. The private dataset includes cases, construction code, manifest, exclusions, scorer, usage instructions, and aggregate/per-case diagnostic labels. Training data remains private.

This is a failure-enriched validation set repeatedly used during development and selection. It is not an untouched test or representative BFCL sample. Task-ID separation does not establish absence from the initializer's earlier training; original source records lack task-content hashes. The frozen histories were collected under an earlier harness, whereas live task evaluation uses Pi. No cross-harness learning claim follows from that combination.

## Online training protocol

All completed candidates start independently from [Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery/tree/850a32627724d274004241dd10f6cb46fd3f6f83), the prior BFCL `.304/hf/step-1` export, with a frozen reference. The selected run is `2026.10.12.2`, export `global_step_4`; suffixes identify dated run versions, not numbers of optimizer updates.

The loop samples fresh continuations from historical training-only prefixes. At most one repeated-opener boundary per response supplies a target. The rejected token is the repeated opener. Accepted alternatives must be among the captured top-20 candidates and decode to `{` after whitespace trimming. Candidate filtering uses relative `min_p=0.01` and at most 20 accepted tokens. A legal opening brace does not prove that the remaining call will be valid. Empty-target batches skip the optimizer.

FTPO applies a selected-position logit-margin preference loss. For chosen-minus-rejected logit difference `d`, its margin-2 term is `softplus(2-d) * clamp((2-d)/2, 0, 1)`, averaged over accepted alternatives. Frozen-reference squared-logit regularization uses `lambda_mse=0.4`, targeted-token `lambda_mse_target=0.05`, and target deadband `tau_mse_target=0.5`. Token-frequency balancing strengths are 0.3 for rejected tokens and 0.5 for chosen tokens. The pinned implementation defines masking and global weighted normalization. The stronger-regularization run changes `lambda_mse` to 0.8.

No critic, learned reward model, or PPO task-reward objective is used. Fresh generation makes the continuations on-policy; the conditioning histories remain fixed historical replays. This is not full multi-turn on-policy task training. A one-token supervision target still requires model forward/backward computation and changes shared parameters.

| Setting | Executed configuration |
| --- | --- |
| Optimizer | AdamW, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, gradient clip 0.5 |
| Learning rate | Constant `4e-6`; runs `2026.10.12.3` and `.4` use `2e-6`; no warmup |
| Batch | 16 prompts, 2 continuations each, one update epoch; train/forward microbatch 2 |
| Allocation | 192 H100s: policy 120, reference 64, inference 8 |
| Parallelism | Policy pipeline 15 × expert 8; reference pipeline 8 × expert 8; TP/CP/SP 1, no packing |
| Generation | Seed 42, temperature 1, top-p 1, 8,192 new tokens; 73,728-token serving window |
| Diagnostic stop | `</tool_call>` retained in output; special tokens retained; no constrained decoding |
| Evaluation cadence | Initial, every two configured steps, and final; one-step smokes also evaluate at step 1 |
| Live task harness | Pi 0.87.0, chat-template thinking format, Daytona, 32 concurrent trials; 2 CPU/4 GiB RAM/10 GiB disk; trial timeout 1,800 seconds, verifier 300 seconds |

Raw-token protocol replay needs no container. Live BFCL/Pi task evaluation uses Daytona. Checkpoint step numbers must be distinguished from applied updates: the selected four-step run applied three updates and skipped one zero-signal batch.

The replay diagnostic uses temperature 1, top-p 1, seed 42, and an 8,192-token budget, with exactly one fresh continuation per prefix at each checkpoint. Training uses two continuations per prompt. “Single-sample” refers to one evaluated continuation per case, without repeated-generation uncertainty measurement.

Exact retained configs: https://gist.github.com/penfever/76cd73ba893caf0e1b734c625f4e22b4 and https://gist.github.com/penfever/1aae120f47647a2b34df69a62863a89e. These include source, resolved launch, and captured live-resolved files, with byte hashes and caveats about historical storage paths and attempt IDs. Runtime defaults absent from YAML are listed in the gist README and pinned source. Private data and cluster dependencies prevent a public one-command rerun.

## Results measurement

The protocol diagnostic assigns the first applicable category: repeated opener, malformed JSON, invalid generic call envelope, missing/misplaced closer, or valid first-call syntax. The envelope requires a nonempty string `name` and object-valued `arguments`. This does not check tool availability, its argument schema, execution, or later calls. The packaged scorer independently reproduced all 468 retained diagnostic labels at selected-run steps 0, 2, and 4.

| Selected run, configured step | Repeated opener | Malformed JSON | Invalid envelope | Missing/misplaced closer | Valid |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 72 | 27 | 23 | 13 | 21 |
| 2 | 11 | 47 | 47 | 17 | 34 |
| 4 | 1 | 58 | 42 | 13 | 42 |

Among the 72 cases initially labeled repeated opener, final labels were 12 valid, 36 malformed JSON, 19 invalid envelope, four missing/misplaced closer, and one repeated opener. Every one of those 19 invalid envelopes lacked `arguments`. Many malformed responses still contain repeated marker-like content or `$LANG`. Reducing the first visible error does not imply a complete repair.

Standalone exported-checkpoint evaluation measures BFCL-Parity/Pi task success, MATH-500 accuracy, HumanEval+ pass@1, and IFBench loose-prompt accuracy. The full panel sizes are 123, 500, 164, and 300. Serving and evaluation configs are held constant across the baseline and final candidates except checkpoint identity. Inline BFCL trials are separate samples with explicit unscored cases; they are not substituted for standalone results.

| Model/run | BFCL-Parity/Pi | MATH-500 | HumanEval+ | IFBench Loose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Recovery baseline | 30/123 (24.39%) | 457/500 (91.4%) | 52.44% | 82/300 (27.33%) |
| `2026.10.12.1` | 44/123 (35.77%) | 466/500 (93.2%) | 73.78% | 72/300 (24.00%) |
| `2026.10.12.2`, released | 43/123 (34.96%) | 461/500 (92.2%) | 68.90% | 78/300 (26.00%) |
| `2026.10.12.3` | 32/123 (26.02%) | 464/500 (92.8%) | 69.51% | 79/300 (26.33%) |
| `2026.10.12.4` | 37/123 (30.08%) | 466/500 (93.2%) | 70.73% | 84/300 (28.00%) |

All standalone cases in this table were scored. For the released checkpoint, six MATH responses had no extractable answer and scored zero; BFCL recorded no errors. Run `.4` had two BFCL agent timeouts scored as failures and two unanswered MATH cases scored zero. Infrastructure exceptions in inline trials remain unscored and visible in the results tracker.

## Decision log and limitations

Integration attempts exposed dependency bootstrapping, microbatch, timeout, raw-token response, installed-tool wrapping, text-block grading, zero-update checkpoint, export, and invalid-argument transcript issues. Their configs and results remain in the tracker. Six completed learning candidates followed: two one-update smokes, a two-update run, the selected four-step run, a lower-rate run, and a stronger-reference-penalty run. They are not independent-seed replications.

The selected run met the campaign's 90% repeated-opener reduction target. Run `.4` reached 84.7%, with 28 valid first calls versus `.2`'s 42 and lower BFCL success, although `.4` outperformed `.2` on all three ancillary benchmarks. This motivated selecting `.2`. The two-update `.1` had the highest standalone BFCL score but only 81.7% opener reduction and the largest IFBench Loose decline among these candidates. The separate tracker gives each candidate's configured steps, applied updates, learning rate, and regularization.

IFBench Loose became the primary IF measure after trace inspection showed sensitivity to formatting and checker behavior; Strict remains a secondary measurement. This metric change occurred during the study and is not preregistered. Some strict failures reflect genuine instruction violations; others expose weak or mismatched validators. Loose does not remove all those defects. The IF follow-up preserves the original measurements and proposes an independently validated benchmark.

No repeated-generation unchanged-model control, masked-SFT arm, cross-harness transfer panel, or independently measured production tensor/logit equivalence was completed. Capability non-inferiority margins were not specified or demonstrated. Weight publication verified export bytes and all 39 weight shards; that is distinct from proving training/inference numerical equivalence. Some W&B runs report stale or crashed status despite successful Iris completion and retained final traces; the results use retained artifacts and actual-update evidence.

## Code and artifacts

Result posts: [figure and private-benchmark access](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043#issuecomment-6124431515); [complete retained-results tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043#issuecomment-6124432248).

- Marin [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) contains the campaign; stacked [#10058](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10058) contains closeout/review fixes. Both are open at publication. The selected run used Marin `3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6`; later code fixes must not be treated as part of that executed revision.
- MarinSkyRL merged changes: [#887 FTPO](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887), [#970 DPO/validation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/970), [#971 installed-agent engine integration](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/971), [#972 Daytona credentials](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/972), [#973 replay sessions](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/973), [#974 repeated-opener target](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/974), [#975 boundary selection](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/975), [#976 raw token prefixes](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/976), [#977 tool normalization](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/977), [#978 grading pin](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/978), [#979 training replay/checkpoint fixes](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/979), and [#980 grading pin](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/980).
- Harbor merged changes: [#255 native exact-token capture](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/255), [#256 correlation IDs](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/256), [#257 proxy cleanup](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/257). The configs specify executed dependency pins; these links include supporting and later closeout changes.
- Final training runtime: [MarinSkyRL `37ec019`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/37ec019b756cfd988ca8abd042cf25f24934224b). Capability evaluator: [Evalchemy `97fffeb`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/tree/97fffeb7df60875c5a5c14ec215dd4e7683102c5). No new Evalchemy change is claimed for this campaign.
- Public aggregate evidence and figure: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Protocol-FTPO-Results/tree/a7bbbfbe05e16ee5cadbbcdd8135fbf59b40cfb7. Exact configs: https://gist.github.com/penfever/76cd73ba893caf0e1b734c625f4e22b4; integration attempts: https://gist.github.com/penfever/1aae120f47647a2b34df69a62863a89e. The benchmark link above requires access. Raw replay prefixes and training data are not included in the public artifacts.
- Follow-ups: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060 and https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061.

## Conclusion

This run supports a narrow result: a selected-position preference intervention can sharply reduce a repeated-opener signature on fixed held-out-from-this-training histories. Most responses still fail full first-call syntax, and capability preservation is unproven. The campaign closes with a public checkpoint, public measurements, and a private reproducibility dataset. Remaining experiments are tracked in the linked follow-ups; closing this issue does not assert that all original proposal criteria were met.

<details>
<summary>Original proposal, preserved for scope comparison</summary>

Design, implement, execute, and validate online feedback loops that target specific model failures at the smallest justified token or action span. Start with tool-call closure: after a complete valid payload, prefer a harness-accepted closing sequence over an observed invalid continuation. An open but still-valid prefix is not a failure.

The BFCL recovery campaign's extended DPO run fell from 34/123 successful Pi trials to 0/123 after eight updates. Whole-trajectory preferences did not preserve tool behavior. [Public analysis and artifacts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/tree/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b).

Reuse the online final-token preference optimization (FTPO) path in [MarinSkyRL #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887) where appropriate. [Dr. Doom](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691) demonstrated reduced repetitive tails, but its alternative-token selection does not verify tool repairs. FTPO already supplies exact-token candidates, a selected-position preference objective, frozen-reference logit regularization, and empty-window optimizer skipping. Its supported topology excludes TP>1, context parallelism, sequence parallelism, and packing.

Done when:

- Define separate failure predicates and positive-evidence requirements for closure, argument repair, repeated-error recovery, and eventual progress/finalization. Implement and validate closure first; mark the other behaviors as separate subsequent experiments rather than blending them into one reward.
- Preserve the exact conditioning tokens, harness/tool schema, model version, and verification evidence. A positive candidate must be valid under the same prefix. Admit verified candidates outside rollout top-K; support a short span when a delimiter is multi-token.
- Connect on-policy generation, target construction, actual optimizer updates, weight synchronization, and fresh generation in MarinSkyRL. Reuse existing roles/checkpointing; no critic or learned reward model is required for parser-verifiable cases.
- Run a Pi-only smoke and a bounded learning experiment on training-complement tasks. Compare local preference learning with positive-only masked SFT on the same repairs and an unchanged-model control. Record skipped versus applied updates and compute costs.
- Evaluate held-out protocol validity, accepted/executed calls, premature closure, repetition, and task solve rate before and after training. Evaluate other harnesses to measure transfer; do not infer transfer from Pi alone. Keep BFCL-Parity out of mined training targets.
- Publish pinned configuration, provenance, failure examples cleared for redistribution, and results including regressions. State that token-local supervision changes shared model weights and does not guarantee globally local effects or one-token compute cost.

[Campaign closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040); related work: [datakit local-pair mining #10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042) and [online multi-harness integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041). [Detailed proposed interventions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-repair-versus-online-rl-20261011.md).

</details>

topics.title: Preserve BFCL recovery and shared-engine agent support
topics.body:
Preserve the BFCL recovery campaign's collection, preference curation, DPO, checkpoint export, and Daytona operations support. Retain task-split and trace provenance checks, assistant-only masks, and explicit treatment of malformed or repeated tool calls in preference data. Preserve explicit sharding in Snowball token reshapes and support CPU exports with a selected weight dtype and revision-pinned tokenizer.

Allow installed agents to request model turns through the shared RolloutEngine while it owns task machines, isolated grading, and exact-token training records. Support exact token-prefix replay and build versioned protocol diagnostics from BFCL tasks reserved and excluded from training before failure selection. The diagnostic checks tool-call syntax separately from task success.

Add BFCL training subsets checked against pinned task-content hashes and disjoint validation IDs. Pin task container images by digest and run grading in a separate machine that holds private grading files. Add a configurable final-token preference optimization (FTPO) recipe with the Pi agent, Daytona containers, BFCL-Parity task validation, and protocol diagnostic validation. Pin merged https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/980 at 37ec019b756cfd988ca8abd042cf25f24934224b. Its tree matches tested commit cb98adde74f1ee1c607e18e77d08483f3ae37ec0 and adds the repaired grading dependencies to the preceding PR #979 runtime. The training-token selector handles repeated `<tool_call>` openers separated by whitespace, including a first opener in the frozen assistant prompt. It also initializes missing optimizer state before a zero-update checkpoint save. Smoke `.13`, on the preceding runtime, saved a native checkpoint after one optimizer update; the zero-update case remains unverified in a live run.

Build training replays from task IDs assigned to training in the diagnostic's fixed split manifest. Check archive, tokenizer, and partition hashes; retain exact token prefixes and source-record identities; select the smallest prefix SHA-256 per task. Exclusions must specify a source-record ID and its exact conversion error. Collect all other conversion errors before rejecting the build. Input version `2026.10.11.4` contains 581 training prefixes from distinct tasks, 123 BFCL-Parity cases, and 156 diagnostic cases. Both validation sets are unchanged from version `2026.10.11.3`. Training and diagnostic prefix continuations do not execute tools. BFCL-Parity runs the Pi agent and its tools in Daytona containers.

Disable transitive uv source overrides in the isolated SkyRL launcher. A live smoke failed before GPU submission when a Git workspace supplied a development dependency below SkyRL's required version. The launch-composition tests now exercise the production bootstrap.

Reject explicitly unequal Megatron forward and training microbatches before submission. The next smoke allocated 192 GPUs before the runtime validator found this mismatch. The campaign now derives its forward microbatch from its training role plan. All 30 launcher tests and prepare-mode validation pass. Neither failed smoke reached model inference or training.

Scripted Daytona probes matched original grading in nine oracle/wrong/missing comparisons across three images in each of the training and evaluation accounts. The campaign evidence and remaining validation limits are recorded in #10040. Includes the Daytona runbook from #9858.

Set Pi's required `thinking_format` to `chat-template` for the hosted inference endpoint. Real Pi construction and prepare-mode validation pass. A live smoke exposed double-wrapped function definitions at the installed-agent boundary. The SkyRL pin converts these tools to the session's flat schema; its adapter-to-model-client regression and 2,504 CPU tests pass, with nine skipped.

A live Pi smoke generated model responses but failed BFCL grading because Pi supplies user content as text blocks. Normalize those blocks before constructing typed grading evidence. Preserve non-object JSON tool arguments as transcript evidence so file-based graders can run after rejected calls. Execution and final-action submissions still require argument objects; invalid JSON still fails at ingestion. A saved failing BFCL transcript now converts without changing its decoded arguments. Local tests cover correct and incorrect output files after a rejected call.

The grading repair passed 103 rollout tests and 497 TaskCompendium tests. One TaskCompendium failure depends on case-sensitive filenames and reproduces on unchanged main on this Mac. The affected workspace lane recorded 4,077 passes and four task-curation failures that also reproduce on main; the Haliax lane passed 387 tests. A review follow-up reuses Verifyit's duplicate-key decoder hook; 116 rollout and protocol tests pass. Adding that direct dependency to the lockfile selects the broad root suite. That run recorded 2,717 passes, the four task-curation failures, and one missing-bubblewrap collection error also reproduced on main. Lint and type checks pass. Run `2026.10.12.3` completed grading and retained scored and unscored validation records.

Request HF-format exports at checkpoint intervals and training end in the FTPO recipe. Smoke `.13` completed an optimizer update and saved a native checkpoint, but its coordinator failed during terminal export because the explicit callback list omitted export requests. A direct callback check now verifies checkpoint and export requests at terminal step 1, before the regular two-step interval is due. Run `2026.10.12.3` completed training and HF-format export, including verification of all 39 export shards and metadata consistency.

Expose learning rate and FTPO reference-regularization coefficient as required experiment inputs. Run `2026.10.12.3` completed four optimizer updates and reduced repeated tool-call openers from 69 to 3 among 156 diagnostic cases. Compared with the Recovery initializer, its matched policy evaluations improved MATH-500, HumanEval+, and BFCL-Parity, while IFBench strict-prompt accuracy declined from 73/300 to 68/300. Capability preservation remains unproven. Candidate `2026.10.12.4` changes only `lambda_mse` from 0.4 to 0.8. It passed prepare-mode validation but has not run.

topics.title: [grafana] Alert on failed hero attempts during retry initialization
topics.body:
An unexpected failure of a hero training attempt can be followed by an Iris retry without a critical Grafana alert during the interruption. `TrainingProgressStalled` resets its clock for the new execution and allows 45 minutes for initialization. `TrainingTelemetryGone` stops firing when the retry publishes `phase=initializing`. The warning-only `task_retried` check requires fresh training telemetry and an event from the last 15 minutes, so it can miss a retry that takes longer to initialize.

A [September 30 checkpoint failure](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/570) resumed training about 27 minutes after the last completed step. Neither critical rule fired during that gap. The checkpoint failure's initiating cause remains unconfirmed.

Done when: an unexpected failed attempt or retry of an enrolled hero run produces a critical alert during the interruption, including while its replacement initializes. Cover retry, recovery, and duplicate-notification behavior in tests.

topics.title: Build an instruction-following benchmark with validated output contracts
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Build and validate an instruction-following benchmark whose checks implement the stated instructions and distinguish formatting compliance from answer quality. The [localized FTPO campaign #10043](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043) found real instruction failures alongside checker weaknesses in IFBench. Keep its official scores in the record; do not remove cases because a preferred model fails them.

## Description

The Recovery baseline scored 82/300 on IFBench loose-prompt accuracy. Runs `2026.10.12.2`, `.3`, and `.4` scored 78, 79, and 84. Strict accuracy for `.2` and `.3` was 68/300 versus baseline 73/300. Loose normalizes some formatting differences but does not fix the underlying constraint validators. These observations do not establish general instruction-following regression or preservation.

The trace audit used [Evalchemy `97fffeb`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/tree/97fffeb7df60875c5a5c14ec215dd4e7683102c5), specifically [grader.py](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/97fffeb7df60875c5a5c14ec215dd4e7683102c5/eval/chat_benchmarks/IFBench/grader.py) and [instructions.py](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/97fffeb7df60875c5a5c14ec215dd4e7683102c5/eval/chat_benchmarks/IFBench/instructions.py). The public campaign report and result tracker contain measured scores; trace archives remain access-controlled.

The numeric IDs below are evaluator `doc_id` values in the retained `allenai/IFBench_test` records, not asserted universal dataset IDs. The evaluator loaded the dataset without an explicit Hub revision; no immutable upstream dataset revision is asserted. Exact prompt comparisons were made against the retained evaluation artifacts. A replacement must pin both data and checker versions.

Observed issues to turn into regression fixtures:

- List-marker tasks 83/84: the checker counts the special marker anywhere, although its description requires line starts. Missing or altered `!?!?` markers are also genuine failures and must remain failures.
- Nested-bracket tasks 106/111: accumulated depth can satisfy the checker without a fully balanced structure. In task 106 a disordered 197,987-character baseline response passed, while a 2,144-character candidate response answering the math question failed the structural condition. Semantic usefulness and structural compliance need separate scores.
- Quotation tasks 115/117 and 123/124: quote adjacency, nesting, and whitespace handling can interact with explanatory text. Define the exact accepted language and validate it with independent fixtures.
- HTML task 138: one italic region plus text can pass without satisfying the requested coverage of sections.
- Palindrome task 234: occurrence counting can reward repetition rather than distinct qualifying words; the baseline passed with 50 repeated occurrences.
- Stopword task 176: the Recovery response had 5,576 characters; run `2026.10.12.3` passed with 289,654 characters. Constraint satisfaction alone does not capture usefulness, repetition, or bounded completion.
- Option-only tasks 100/103: duplicated options or added explanation violate the instruction. These are positive controls for genuine model failure, not benchmark defects.

The `.3` model had 12 strict losses and seven gains relative to baseline; 11 of the losses involved formatting constraints. Eight losses were shared with `.2`. Responses over 100,000 characters fell from 50 at baseline to 13 in `.2` and 20 in `.3`, so a uniform verbosity increase does not explain the results. Stored responses contain reasoning-like prose, but the audit did not independently prove a reasoning-channel extraction bug.

## Hypothesis or goal

A benchmark with explicit output contracts, independently tested validators, and separate semantic/format measures will better detect useful instruction-following changes than a single aggregate pass rate over weak constraints.

## Status and proposed experiment

Proposed; no new data collection or training is launched by this issue.

1. Specify whether each instruction applies to final-answer content, the whole visible response, or structured output. Test reasoning/final-channel extraction independently. Do not silently strip content to improve a model's score.
2. Publish a versioned taxonomy covering exact choice, counts, ordering, formatting, structured outputs, multi-constraint composition, and semantic requirements. Define ambiguous instructions before collecting labels.
3. Build validator fixtures with valid alternative answers, near misses, malformed structures, repeated garbage, quoted markers, and adversarial counterexamples. Use metamorphic tests: changes irrelevant to an instruction should preserve its label. Cross-check structural validators with an independent implementation.
4. Report semantic task correctness separately from literal contract compliance. Measure output length, repetition, truncation, extraction failures, and infrastructure coverage. A short answer is not automatically correct; a long answer is not automatically incorrect.
5. Split by task/template family before generating variants. Reserve new held-out compositions and constraint combinations. Do not tune validators or choose examples against only the released FTPO checkpoint.
6. Evaluate Recovery, the released Protocol-FTPO model, and diverse comparison models under fixed serving settings and matched budgets. Repeat generations, publish paired uncertainty estimates, and predeclare acceptable regression margins. Retain official IFBench Strict and Loose as reference panels.

Done when the dataset, validator source, adversarial fixtures, versioned protocol, and model comparison are published with provenance and redistribution clearance; observed IFBench defects have reproducible fixtures; and the report distinguishes corrected measurement from changed model ability. If the replacement is not more reliable, report that result.

## Links

- Parent experiment: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043
- Related protocol-composition experiment: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061
- Public campaign evidence: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Protocol-FTPO-Results/tree/a7bbbfbe05e16ee5cadbbcdd8135fbf59b40cfb7

## Decision log

The parent campaign changed its primary IF metric to Loose after inspecting traces. This follow-up keeps both official scores and tests a replacement without retroactively relabeling the parent results.

## Conclusion

Pending benchmark validation and comparative evaluation.

topics.title: Test composable tool-protocol skills with localized supervision
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Extend the repeated-opener experiment into separately measured JSON, call-envelope, and closure skills. Use final-token preference optimization (FTPO) only for provably wrong local token transitions. Compare short masked-supervised repair spans where correctness needs several tokens. Test staged introduction with continued replay of earlier skills against matched joint and serial schedules.

## Description

In [#10043](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043), run `2026.10.12.2` reduced repeated openers 72→1/156 but raised valid first calls only 21→42/156. Among the 72 original repeaters, 36 became malformed JSON, 19 invalid envelopes, four missing/misplaced closers, 12 valid, and one remained repeated. All 19 invalid envelopes lacked `arguments`. The intervention changed the first error without generally completing valid calls.

The existing FTPO path selects at most one boundary per response and accepts captured alternatives whose decoded text trims to `{`. It does not verify full-call repair. The legacy scorer checks first-call JSON, a generic `name`/`arguments` envelope, and a close marker; it does not check the exposed tool schema or execution. Reference regularization did not establish global capability preservation.

## Hypothesis or goal

Parser- and schema-verified local supervision can teach additional protocol skills. Retaining earlier skills during later training may reduce regression. The experiment must distinguish improved complete-call behavior from shifting the first observed error or avoiding tool calls.

## Status and design

Proposed follow-up to the completed campaign. This issue does not launch training. It carries forward the 2026-10-12 protocol-skill-composition design, with the following implementation and experiment requirements.

### Validator and labels

Build a versioned, stateful validator with three layers: conversation protocol, JSON syntax, and the actual exposed tool schema. Start with the current Hermes/Pi contract and add harness-specific adapters explicitly. Track strings, escapes, nested objects/arrays, duplicate keys, argument types, required properties, enums, and additional-property policy. Require required fields; do not force optional fields to appear.

Here Hermes denotes the model's tool-call serialization, such as `<tool_call>{"name":"shell","arguments":{"command":"pwd"}}</tool_call>`. Pi is the agent harness that executes the call. The active schema determines which tool names and arguments are legal; this example does not define a universal harness contract. Masked supervised learning applies loss only to the selected correct repair span.

Distinguish valid complete calls, incomplete but extendable prefixes, and prefixes that cannot become valid without changing an earlier token. An open brace or token delimiter is not itself an error. Braces in strings, shell commands, tool output, and quoted examples must not be treated as global structural delimiters. Truncation is a separate bounded-completion failure, not proof that the last token was illegal.

For each observed violation, retain the earliest provably illegal transition and its exact conditioning token IDs. If a missing field becomes detectable only at closure, do not assume the closer caused the defect. Locate a justified earlier edit or exclude the example. Validate a candidate's complete decoded bytes in context, including tokenizer-merged punctuation. Several next tokens can be admissible.

### Data and learning method

Use training-approved BFCL traces and fresh continuations from training-only prefixes. Split by task before creating variants; keep legacy diagnostic, parity, and capability-evaluation examples out of training. Preserve tokenizer/template/schema/validator hashes, source task/call, exact prefix, rejected token/span, accepted alternatives, masks, verification evidence, and exclusions.

- Use FTPO for repeated openers, illegal separators, extra braces, or wrong closers only when the same prefix supports a provably valid alternative.
- Start with loss-masked supervised learning for multi-token envelope or field repairs. Compare a local span preference objective as a separate ablation. Avoid recreating whole-trajectory length imbalance.
- Construct repairs only when unchanged history and schema determine them. Do not invent argument values or tool intent. Label syntax-only evidence separately from execution-verified repair.
- Mine natural failures and separately report deterministic corruptions of verified valid calls. Measure unique tasks, prefixes, family counts, repair lengths, ambiguity exclusions, and valid-candidate coverage before estimating training scale.
- Measure top-K misses and empty-target skips. Add explicit off-top-K token scoring only if coverage requires it, with numerical/alignment tests. Multi-token repairs may use teacher-forced repaired histories, labeled as such and capped per source call.

### Benchmark and experiment arms

Keep the legacy 156-case diagnostic unchanged. Add frozen held-out prefixes after openers, within nested structures/strings, between fields, before required fields, after valid payloads, and at message termination. Include already-correct cases, optional-field omissions, quoted markers, premature-closure traps, unseen schema shapes, and deeper nesting. Keep unconstrained decoding as the primary evaluation; grammar-constrained decoding is a separately labeled control.

Report local-boundary admissibility, unconditional complete-call validity, unconstrained full-rollout behavior, and task/capability outcomes separately. The main syntax endpoint requires valid JSON, schema, and protocol within the budget. Retain first-error labels for comparison and report later stages as not evaluable when blocked. Include paired transitions, initially-valid retention, call counts, trailing content, length, truncation, non-marker repetition, and coverage. Schema accuracy conditional on parsing must not replace full-validity over all attempts.

1. Freeze data, parser, initializer/reference, serving settings, and budgets. Use Recovery at `850a32627724d274004241dd10f6cb46fd3f6f83` for matched arms unless a new initialization decision is explicitly recorded.
2. Run a short closer-only FTPO experiment for complete valid payloads followed by an invalid close transition. Verify labels and learnability before adding families.
3. Compare closer-only with an opener-plus-closer mixture at the same update, total-boundary, learning-rate, and regularization budget. Report the reduced per-family exposure in the mixed arm.
4. Add JSON and envelope families one at a time. Compare masked supervised repair with preference repair before combining loss types. Begin with fixed family sampling and per-task caps; record effective weights after token-frequency balancing.
5. Compare pure serial, balanced joint, and staged-with-replay schedules with matched total per-family exposures and optimizer budgets. Evaluate all established skills at each checkpoint. Do not adapt sampling repeatedly to held-out results.
6. Use an unchanged-model repeated-generation control and matched SFT arm. Measure other harnesses separately before claiming transfer. Retain BFCL/Pi, MATH-500, HumanEval+, and IFBench Loose (Strict secondary), with a later replacement linked below.

Do not begin with a bespoke weighted sum of several loss types or gradient-conflict machinery. Validate each path first; homogeneous interleaved batches still require loss-scale and update-contribution measurements. Valid examples need a supported imitation/reference preservation objective, not fabricated negative tokens.

### Gates

Before GPU runs, independently test complete-call validation against the incremental parser; cover escapes, nesting, duplicate keys, optional/required fields, unknown tools, merged tokens, split delimiters, reasoning boundaries, truncation, and corrupted prefixes. Verify supervised-token alignment and global normalization across microbatches. These are verification requirements, not claims of existing distributed bugs.

Select checkpoints by complete-call validity and per-family retention. Retain the legacy repeated-opener gate: at least 90% reduction in repeated-opener failures relative to fresh generations from the unchanged initializer on the same 156 prefixes, reported as `1 - final_failures / initial_failures`. Define opportunity sets and gates for new failure families before training; do not silently extend that denominator to all closers or average families together. Predeclare acceptable capability and earlier-skill regression margins. Use paired uncertainty and repeated samples; lack of a significant difference does not establish non-inferiority. Archive traces before stopping a degrading run. Most syntax replay needs no containers; execution checks use Daytona, the container service used in the parent campaign.

Done when versioned validators/data, matched ablations, complete-call and capability results, failed/skipped target counts, costs, configs, and code are published or access-controlled with explicit reasons; and the conclusion states whether compositional gains survive unconstrained rollouts and prior-skill retention.

## Links

- Parent experiment: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043
- IF benchmark follow-up: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060
- [FTPO implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/37ec019b756cfd988ca8abd042cf25f24934224b/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/ftpo.py), [configuration](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/37ec019b756cfd988ca8abd042cf25f24934224b/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/config/ftpo.py), [legacy protocol scorer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ea07f68d79d25ca268b78913d66383667448d70/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/tool_protocol.py).
- Public campaign evidence: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Protocol-FTPO-Results/tree/a7bbbfbe05e16ee5cadbbcdd8135fbf59b40cfb7
- Adjacent work: [offline local-pair mining #10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042), [multi-harness integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041).

## Decision log

Start with valid-payload closure and an opener-retention mixture. General task progress and argument semantics need environment evidence and remain separate from syntax repair.

## Conclusion

Pending implementation and matched experiments. The parent result establishes only repeated-opener reduction on the legacy diagnostic.
