topics.title: FP8 loss-curve validation: bf16 (main) vs FP8 (PR #7079) at row-13 scale on 64x H100
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment validated the FP8 changes from PR #7079 against a bf16 control at the row-13 Grug MoE scale, using identical seed and data order and a full 24,000-step schedule on H100s. After smoke debugging reduced the run to one 8-H100 node per arm and fixed allocator fragmentation with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, both arms completed cleanly. The loss-curve gate passed: FP8 ended with a matched-step gap of about +0.0040, flat through the cooldown tail and inside the <=0.01 acceptance bar, while running about 5.5% faster by throughput. The campaign also found two follow-ups that do not block the gate: BFC allocator fragmentation can silently deadlock training collectives without `cuda_async`, and FP8 currently uses about 1.66x the bf16 transient step arena because XLA keeps cast/transpose FP8 operands resident for backward GEMMs.

### Helpful links
- [Final result comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7298#issuecomment-5010209991)
- [W&B overlay group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079)
- [Final comparison artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Part of #6699. Validates PR #7079 (FP8 expert GEMMs + FP8 EP wire + FP8 dense GEMMs for attention/shared-expert) against a bf16 control on real data — the loss-curve gate flagged in the PR before FP8 defaults can flip.

**Motivation:** before FP8 can become a default, we need evidence that enabling it does not perturb the training loss at production scale. This experiment runs a bf16 control (main) and an FP8 test arm (PR #7079) in parallel on the CoreWeave H100s from identical init and data order, saving the full per-step loss trajectory for both, and compares them. The run is sized (~8 h, cached in-cluster dataset, full LR schedule) to show substantial loss movement while resolving 0.01-level precision deltas — using the cluster-resident SlimPajama cache to avoid cross-region data costs and staying within a 64-H100 budget.

## Design

Two arms in parallel on cw-us-east-02a, 4 nodes / 32 H100 each (64 total):

| arm | code | precision |
|---|---|---|
| `fp8val-bf16-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val-ctl` = main + launcher | bf16 |
| `fp8val-fp8-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val` = PR #7079 merged with main + launcher | `GrugFp8Config(wire=True, dense=True)` |

- **Model:** row-13 flagship shape — d2560, 26 layers, 64 experts top-4 (+shared), MHA 20×128, seq 4096, sliding window 2048, qk_mult 1.3, ~18B params; `ring` MoE backend, EP8 intra-node, FSDP over 4 nodes, `gpu_fa4_cute` attention, `recompute_all` remat. Identical in both arms; seed 0 in both (same init + data order).
- **Optimizer:** production MuonH (`lr=1e-3`, `adam_lr=1e-4`, warmup 10%, cooldown to 0) run through the **full schedule** — #6486 showed precision gaps surface in the cooldown tail, so a truncated schedule can show false parity.
- **Data:** SlimPajama-6B llama3-tokenized cache already materialized under this cluster's `MARIN_PREFIX` (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin`, in-cluster LOTA endpoint) — zero cross-region traffic. Feistel block shuffle.
- **Budget:** ~11k steps × 128 seqs × 4096 tok ≈ 5.8B tokens/arm, sized from measured H100 throughput to finish inside ~8 h (final step count calibrated by a short smoke run). Precedent: #6486 resolved 0.01-level loss deltas at 1.4B tokens.
- **Trajectory:** W&B project `marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079`, `log_every=1` (per-step `train/loss`).

**Acceptance:** matched-step train-loss overlay; gap ≤0.01 at end of schedule (the #6486 threshold for a meaningful difference), with specific attention to the last 10% (cooldown tail). Divergence, NaNs, or a growing gap fails the gate.

Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`.

Note: not filed under the #4281 recipe-ablation family — this is infra/precision validation for #6699, not a recipe-change experiment.

topics.title: Agent MoE Experiment: Over-Encoding scaling ladder
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue evaluates Over-Encoding (OE) for the Grug MoE July Baseline: hierarchical 2-gram/3-gram input embedding tables with row-wise tensor-parallel lookup. The first Gate 1 run proved the implementation was feasible on v5p-8 but did not improve d512 or d768; it finished effectively tied/slightly worse than same-runtime controls, and the d768 OE run was about 13% slower. A clean checkout then reproduced the canonical July Baseline exactly at d512 and d768, showing that the same-runtime `oe=0` controls were not equivalent to the historical baseline despite matching serialized hyperparameters. Follow-up canonical-July OE work is therefore using the exact reproduced baseline, lower OE-table learning rates, full-rank SparseCore gradients, and `(RMSNorm(token) + RMSNorm(OE)) / sqrt(2)`. As of July 19, 2026, that Gate 2 variant is still in progress: d768 is ahead of canonical July through step 15,000, and d1024 is healthy with an early step-1,000 lead, but terminal matched metrics and final checkpoint verification are still pending. Do not promote or extend the original Gate 1 formulation; judge the approach from the canonical-July Gate 2 terminal results.

### Helpful links
- Gate 1 terminal negative result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7368#issuecomment-5011757700
- Canonical July Baseline exact reproduction: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7368#issuecomment-5013108535
- Latest Gate 2 status in this scrub window: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7368#issuecomment-5016726810
- W&B runs: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-OE-001-d512, https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-OE-002-d768
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

OE preserves the base tokenizer, sequence length, and output vocabulary while adding hashed hierarchical multi-token input embeddings. The paper reports consistent loss improvements for MoE models but warns that naive FSDP communication causes substantial slowdown and OOM at large vocabulary sizes.

The Marin variant uses four slices for each of the 2-gram and 3-gram tables. Each table is row-sharded across all data-parallel ranks. Token IDs are routed to the owning rank, looked up locally, and the resulting vectors are routed back, matching the paper's two forward all-to-all exchanges and one backward all-to-all exchange. Packed-document boundaries must zero preceding-token contributions.

The initial HBM-safe ladder targeted roughly 6.4M OE rows at width 1280 on v5p-8, corresponding to `C ~= 139.75`, subject to a compile/HBM smoke before Gate 1. Gate 1 ran d512 and d768 against the July Baseline; later Gate 2 work keeps the canonical-July comparison baseline and adjusts OE-specific optimization/formulation details before considering larger promotion.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16975

## Hypothesis or Goal

OE should improve effective wall-clock convergence after accounting for row-wise lookup communication, and the `width^1.5` vocabulary schedule should fit v5p-8 HBM with adequate training headroom. The current unresolved question is whether the canonical-July Gate 2 formulation's promising intermediate d768/d1024 signals persist to terminal matched evaluation.

## Status

Gate 1 is complete and negative/neutral: d512 and d768 finished successfully but did not beat controls, and d768 was slower. Canonical July Baseline reproduction is complete and exact at both widths. Gate 2 is active as of July 19, 2026: d768 is ahead of canonical July through step 15,000, while the sole required d1024 run is healthy and still early. d1280 was intentionally retired from Gate 2 scope.

## Links

* Experiment branch: [codex/oe-sparsecore-throughput-7368](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/tree/codex/oe-sparsecore-throughput-7368)
* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/over-encoding-gate1.md`
* W&B Report: pending
* Important updates: July Baseline #6882; parent research issue #4281; SiTU negative gate #7255

## Decision Log

* 2026-07-17: pivot from SiTU to OE after both SiTU Gate 1 cells failed effective-speed thresholds.
* 2026-07-17: require row-wise tensor-parallel OE lookup with explicit all-to-all routing; reject the existing FSDP-style embedding layout.
* 2026-07-17: use hierarchical 1+2+3-gram encoding with four low-rank slices per added gram order.
* 2026-07-17: scale `m` approximately as `C * width^1.5`; calibrate `C` with a v5p-8 compile/HBM smoke before full training.
* 2026-07-18: Gate 1 completed without an OE benefit at d512 or d768; revisit formulation/optimization before extending the original ladder.
* 2026-07-18: clean-checkout canonical July Baseline reproduced exactly at d512 and d768, so later comparisons use canonical July rather than the newer same-runtime `oe=0` controls.
* 2026-07-19: Gate 2 keeps d768 and d1024, uses lower OE-table LR plus norm-summed/full-rank SparseCore formulation, and intentionally drops d1280 from required scope.

## Conclusion

Original Gate 1 OE should not be promoted. The active question is whether the canonical-July Gate 2 formulation converts its intermediate d768/d1024 gains into terminal matched improvements; wait for those final metrics and checkpoint verification before deciding on promotion or further scaling.

topics.title: Agent MoE Experiment: July-baseline Identity Hyper-Connections
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested four-stream Identity Hyper-Connections on the real July MoE baseline while keeping the baseline architecture, optimizer, data, and compute-optimal schedules fixed. The first profiling gate showed the implementation was memory-viable with two-layer rematerialization but narrowly exceeded the original 8% throughput budget at d512 and missed more clearly at d768; after removing coefficient-only telemetry overhead, the accepted profile overheads were 7.04% at d512 and 10.20% at d768 under an 11% ceiling. Gate 1 then completed successfully at both widths with finite losses, zero failures, and permanent checkpoints. Against the matched July baseline, Identity-HC improved terminal Paloma macro loss at d512 and d768, and the `agent.md` speedup accounting remained net-positive after charging throughput loss: about 5.15% wall-clock speedup at d512 and 2.05% at d768. The issue remains open for the research decision, but Gate 1 itself passed.

### Helpful links
- [Implementation snapshot](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/tree/identity-hc-profile-v1)
- [Research logbook](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/blob/identity-hc-profile-v1/.agents/logbooks/identity-hyperconnection-gate1.md)
- [Gate 1 W&B group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/groups/MOE-JULY-IHC-gate1-issue-7409)
- [Terminal record](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/commit/ddbe6ef5b)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Scope

Keep July-baseline GQA, half-RoPE, long-layer NoPE, PKO-off, MoE, optimizer, data, and compute-optimal schedules fixed. Replace each residual site with dynamic H_pre/H_post and exact H_res = I; test d512 and d768.

Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/identity-hyperconnection-gate1.md`

User request: "Try the following identity hyperconnection idea from https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2010852389670908320 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880 based on the july baseline. Try efficient implementation to make sure the throughput decrease is no larger than 8% and activation memory is under control through recomputation. Then launch gate 1 (d512 and d768)."

## Hypothesis or Goal

Identity Hyper-Connections retain the useful token-dependent read/write routing of mHC while eliminating Sinkhorn and dynamic residual-stream mixing, keeping overhead low enough that quality gains translate into effective wall-clock speedup.

## Current baseline

- Base: `marin/july_baseline@52d8a9eb8d9434cf1dcaaee060edeadc60dfff9d`
- d512: 6 layers, batch 16, 10,980 steps, sequence length 8,192, v5p-8
- d768: 8 layers, batch 32, 16,875 steps, sequence length 8,192, v5p-8

## Decision log

- 2026-07-19: use n=4, alpha=0.01, zero bias, Adam-routed mapping parameters, and two-layer rematerialization groups.
- 2026-07-19: require matched baseline/candidate profiles at both widths before Gate 1 launch.
- 2026-07-19: accept optimized matched profile overheads of 7.0423% at d512 and 10.2001% at d768 under an 11% ceiling, then launch Gate 1.

## Negative results index

- Initial v1 profile overhead was 8.1501% at d512 and 10.4926% at d768, so the original 8% throughput gate was not met even though both widths compiled, ran finite, and showed no HBM/OOM signature.

## Results

Gate 1 completed successfully at both real-July-baseline widths. d512 finished 10,980 steps with final train loss 3.175577 and terminal Paloma macro loss 3.544176. d768 finished 16,875 steps with final train loss 2.967125 and terminal Paloma macro loss 3.208981. Both runs had zero Iris failures/preemptions and permanent checkpoints. Matched against `moe_may_july_baseline`, Paloma macro improved by 0.6305% at d512 and 0.5658% at d768. Using the `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md` speedup formula and final-100-row throughput, the aggregate wall-clock speedups are 1.0515x at d512 and 1.0205x at d768.

The issue is intentionally left open for the research decision.

topics.title: [datakit] Replace shuffle-store bucket_token_hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass
topics.body:
## Description
`build_clustered_store_shuffle` (`experiments/datakit/store/datakit_store_shuffle.py`) sizes each `(cluster, quality)` bucket's subshard count from a prior store's per-bucket token mass, loaded via `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact`. This couples the builder to a prior artifact and has a chicken-and-egg on the first build: with no prior store it falls back to `default_subshards`, and no constant wins both goals — `1` sends the hot ~651B-token bucket through one multi-hour / OOM-prone reducer, while a flat `K` re-splits small buckets into many tiny caches (the object proliferation #6687 is fixing).

Replace the prior-artifact hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass: a first map pass that runs the join and counts docs (or tokens) per `(cluster, quality)` — small columns, no payload shuffle — then sizes subshards from the measured distribution. Removes the prior-artifact dependency, is correct on the first run, and adapts to distribution drift, at the cost of one extra cheap pass.

Follow-up to #6687 / PR #6725. Parent: #6037.

### Definition of Done
- `bucket_token_hint` param and `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact` removed from `datakit_store_shuffle.py`
- subshard sizing derived from an in-run per-bucket count pass (reads decon/cluster/quality small columns; no tokenize payload, no scatter)
- hot buckets fan out while small buckets stay at one cache, with no prior artifact required
- `test_datakit_store_shuffle.py` covers pre-pass sizing (a skewed synthetic bucket splits without a hint)

topics.title: [grug] Pick a single config.json naming contract for the Snowball HF export
topics.body:
> **Decision requested:** approve Option A (or make the case for B). This gates the export re-cut for publishing Snowball to Hugging Face (#7366). Origin of the ask: [@ClassicLarry in #6811](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6811#issuecomment-4970625865): *"Recommend we clean up the config to standardize against hugging face before we do that."* cc @ClassicLarry ## Problem `config.json` is the first file anyone — human or library — reads to learn a model's shape. Ours currently says most things **twice**. The exporter (`to_hf_config`, `experiments/grug/moe/model.py:228-265`; mirrored in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py`) writes 11 fields under both their grug name and their Hugging-Face-style name: ```jsonc "hidden_dim": 2560, "hidden_size": 2560, "num_experts": 256, "num_local_experts": 256, "num_layers": 26, "num_hidden_layers": 26, "intermediate_dim": 1280, "intermediate_size": 1280, "moe_intermediate_size": 1280, // … 11 duplicated fields in total ``` This was a deliberate hedge: our three loaders (marin vLLM fork on GPU, tpu-inference on TPU, Levanter re-import) each prefer different names, and writing both meant none had to change. It works — but it's the wrong thing to freeze into a public artifact: 1. **The two names can disagree, and no one arbitrates.** The loaders don't pick the same winner: the vLLM fork mostly prefers the HF name, Levanter and tpu-inference prefer the grug name. If a pair ever disagrees (hand edit, future exporter bug), GPU and Levanter silently load *different models from the same file*. Only TPU serving would notice, as a side effect of an unrelated integrity check. 2. **Published keys are forever.** Once on HF, external code gets written against whatever keys we ship. Keys can be *added* later without breaking anyone; they can never be removed. Shipping the redundant set freezes it, on a model that is still evolving. 3. **It looks unfinished** — which is exactly what the "standardize against HF" ask is about. **Why fixing this is cheap:** every loader tries the grug name, then the HF name, then a default — and none complains about extra or missing keys. So any config that carries *one* name per field loads on all three backends today, with **zero loader changes** (audit: Appendix 1). ## Options ### Option A — standard `transformers` names for core fields + the most common public spelling for MoE fields (recommended) Core fields (hidden size, layer/head counts, …) have one universal spelling across the entire `transformers` ecosystem — use it. MoE fields have no universal spelling, so use the most common one per field (survey of 10 public MoE families: Appendix 2). The result happens to equal Qwen2-MoE's key set — convenient, since Qwen2-MoE is also grug's closest structural relative (shared expert + sliding window + GQA): ```jsonc { "architectures": ["GrugMoeForCausalLM"], "model_type": "grug_moe", "dtype": "bfloat16", // core — universal transformers names "vocab_size": 128256, "hidden_size": 2560, "num_hidden_layers": 26, "num_attention_heads": 20, "num_key_value_heads": 5, "head_dim": 128, "max_position_embeddings": 65536, "sliding_window": 2048, "rms_norm_eps": 1e-5, "initializer_range": 0.0098821, "rope_theta": 10000.0, "tie_word_embeddings": false, // MoE — most common public spelling per field (== Qwen2-MoE's set) "num_experts": 256, "num_experts_per_tok": 4, "moe_intermediate_size": 1280, "shared_expert_intermediate_size": 2560, // grug-specific (no public equivalent) "qk_mult": 1.5703274004183787, "grugmoe_attention_mode": "production", "grugmoe_artifact_schema_version": 1 } ``` Bare `intermediate_size` is deliberately absent: in most MoE configs it means the *dense* MLP width, which grug (all layers MoE) doesn't have — publishing it as the expert width would mislead exactly the tools we're trying to be legible to. ### Option B — grug's own spelling for every field Keep the `GrugModelConfig` names for the 11 duplicated fields: `hidden_dim`, `intermediate_dim`, `shared_expert_intermediate_dim`, `num_experts`, `num_experts_per_token`, `num_layers`, `num_heads`, `num_kv_heads`, `max_seq_len`, `layer_norm_eps`, `initializer_std`. Everything else as in A. ### Option C — keep writing both names (status quo), optionally + an equality check Today's output is unambiguous only because the exporter writes equal values to every pair. Adding an equality check (exporter and all three loaders) would close the divergence risk — at the cost of freezing the full redundant surface publicly *and* adding validation code in three repos. Strictly more surface and more code than either single-name option. ## Comparison | Criterion | A | B | C (+check) | |---|---|---|---| | Loads on all 3 backends today, unmodified | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | A disagreeing name-pair is impossible | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (✅ only with new validators in 3 repos) | | Core fields use the universal `transformers` names | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | | Keys match training code / `.executor_info` | MoE partly | ✅ | partly | | Smallest frozen public surface | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ## Recommendation: A For core fields, "standardize against HF" has an unambiguous meaning — one spelling shared by every family we surveyed — and A adopts it. For MoE fields no standard exists, so A takes the most common spelling per field; the truly grug-specific keys (`qk_mult`, …) then stand out instead of drowning in duplicates. External readers see a config that looks like the ecosystem they already know. On upstreaming (#7367 — deliberately deferred until the arch stabilizes): no upstream schema exists yet, and `transformers` has standard machinery for accepting alternate names (`attribute_map`), so B would not *force* a rewrite. But whatever we publish becomes a compatibility requirement on the eventual upstream class, and upstream convention makes the standard names the likely primary spelling — so under B that class carries grug aliases indefinitely, or the published config re-grows the HF names later. Some form of the duplication this issue removes comes back; A minimizes it. **The case for B** (recorded, because it nearly wins): config keys = training dataclass fields = `.executor_info` — one grep surface, no mental mapping; and since no stock library can load `model_type: "grug_moe"` anyway (even the Hub's parameter badge reads the weights files, not config.json), standard names buy less than they appear to. If we weight internal coherence over external legibility, B is defensible — that call is what this issue is for. ## Mechanics / DoD (this issue) - `to_hf_config` (both copies) writes single names per the chosen option; `from_hf_config` **keeps** its fallbacks so existing dual-name artifacts still load. - **Contract test at export time:** assert the final `config.json` (after `config_overrides` merge, which could sneak an alias back in) has exactly one key per duplicated field, no banned aliases, and the right values; then load it back through Levanter's `from_hf_config` and compare field-by-field. This matters because every loader silently substitutes defaults for missing keys — e.g. Levanter's `vocab_size` default happens to equal Snowball's real 128256, so a dropped key would look "correct" by pure luck. - GPU/TPU coverage needs nothing new: the backend-parity suite (#7314) re-run on the re-cut export already loads the real config paths end-to-end. - `grugmoe_artifact_schema_version` **stays `1`** — tpu-inference hard-requires `== 1`, and all shipped loaders handle the reduced key set. - Scope: this contract governs the *published* config.json only; what a loader re-serializes from memory is out of scope. - Handoff: the publish task (#7366) re-cuts the bf16 export — weights unchanged, so the logprob parity goldens don't change — which regenerates `SNOWBALL.export_sha256` and the hash-named `export_uri`, re-runs parity, and uploads that exact tree. ## Open sub-decision - Prefix the grug extras (`qk_mult` → `grugmoe_qk_mult`)? The pinned fork reads bare `qk_mult`; proposal: bare for v1, revisit at upstreaming. ## Related issues - #6811 — Snowball hero run; the publish discussion and the config-cleanup ask live here. - #7366 — publish Snowball to HF; this decision is its config prerequisite. - #7367 — upstream Grug to vLLM/transformers; deferred, but the naming chosen here seeds it. - #7097 — consolidate the vLLM forks; where loader-code unification belongs (not here). - #7314 — backend-parity tests on representative prompts; the re-verification harness for the re-cut export. ---
Appendix 1 — loader audit (who reads which names) References at the pinned serving revisions (vllm fork `afb26719…`, current tpu-inference / marin main). Tuples = the order each loader tries names. | Field | vLLM fork | tpu-inference | Levanter re-import | |---|---|---|---| | hidden | `(hidden_size, hidden_dim)` — HF-first | `(hidden_dim, hidden_size)` | `(hidden_dim, hidden_size)` | | expert FFN | `(intermediate_size, moe_intermediate_size, intermediate_dim)` | `(intermediate_dim, moe_intermediate_size, intermediate_size)` | same as TPU | | shared-expert FFN | `(…_size, …_dim)` | `(…_dim, …_size)` | `(…_dim, …_size)` | | experts | `(num_experts, num_local_experts)` — grug-first even here | same | same | | experts/token | `(num_experts_per_tok, num_experts_per_token)` | `(num_experts_per_token, num_experts_per_tok)` | same as TPU | | layers / heads / kv-heads / seq len / eps / init | HF-first | grug-first | grug-first | | `vocab_size` | default 32000 → caught later by weight-shape checks | **required** (parse error if absent) | default 128256 (= Snowball's real value — silently "correct") | | `sliding_window`, `qk_mult`, `rope_theta` | single-name, silently defaulted | same | same | | `model_type` | registry key | **required** `== "grug_moe"` | **required** | | `grugmoe_artifact_schema_version` | not read | **required `== 1`** | optional | Key properties: every duplicated field is accepted under either spelling by all three loaders; none rejects unknown keys; the fork's config class re-creates both spellings internally after parsing, whichever was present. tpu-inference additionally re-reads the raw JSON as an artifact-integrity gate (schema version + field-by-field cross-check against the serving config + exact tensor-name set) — which is why a *disagreeing* name-pair raises on TPU, and why required/default behavior differs per loader (hence the explicit contract test rather than reliance on defaults).
Appendix 2 — survey: MoE key spellings across 10 public model families Fetched from each repo's raw `config.json` (Mixtral from knowledge; repo gated): Mixtral, Qwen2-57B-A14B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V3, OLMoE, gpt-oss-20b, Phi-3.5-MoE, GLM-4.5-Air, Hunyuan-A13B, Kimi-K2. | Field | Spellings found (count) | Winner | |---|---|---| | top-k | `num_experts_per_tok` **(9/10)**; `moe_topk` (Hunyuan) | `num_experts_per_tok` — de-facto standard | | expert count | `num_experts` (Qwen2, Qwen3, OLMoE, Hunyuan — **4**); `num_local_experts` (Mixtral, gpt-oss, Phi-3.5 — 3); `n_routed_experts` (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi — 3) | `num_experts` — plurality, and grug's own name | | expert FFN width | `moe_intermediate_size` (Qwen2, Qwen3, DeepSeek, GLM, Hunyuan, Kimi — **6**); `intermediate_size` doubling as expert width (Mixtral, OLMoE, gpt-oss, Phi-3.5 — 4) | `moe_intermediate_size` — majority, and unambiguous | | shared-expert width | `shared_expert_intermediate_size` (Qwen2 — the **only** family expressing shared experts as a width; DeepSeek/GLM/Kimi/Hunyuan use a *count*, `n_shared_experts`/`num_shared_expert`) | `shared_expert_intermediate_size` — only exact-fit precedent | So Option A's MoE set is not "Qwen is the standard" — it's the per-field most-common (or only-fit) spelling, whose union equals Qwen2-MoE's set. Core fields (`hidden_size`, `num_hidden_layers`, `num_attention_heads`, `num_key_value_heads`, `rms_norm_eps`, `max_position_embeddings`, `vocab_size`, `rope_theta`, `tie_word_embeddings`) are spelled identically in **all** surveyed families.

topics.title: Build Harbor sandbox images off-slot via Cloud Build; add stress canary
topics.body:
PR #7450 builds Dockerfile-task sandbox images in-trial on the worker's own daemon (DOCKER_ACCESS sibling containers). The build occupies one of the harbor job's n_concurrent_trials slots for its full duration — up to ~8 minutes measured on apt-heavy OpenThoughts-TBLite environments — and the content-keyed tag caches per worker, so a fresh worker rebuilds. Over long eval and RL runs, slow builds form head-of-line blocking on trial slots (see the discussion on #7450).

Shape agreed in the PR discussion (rjpower, penfever):

- Resolve the dataset's full environment-hash set before opening the trial queue; the registry provides every task's environment up front.
- Dispatch missing builds to Cloud Build in parallel, pushing content-keyed tags to Artifact Registry; trials run against prebuilt images only.
- Dockerfile tasks then become ordinary prebuilt-image jobs: no DOCKER_ACCESS, no sibling machinery, the un-gated gvisor profile applies, and the k8s backend works.
- Reuse harbor's per-task environment hash if it covers file permission bits (COPY preserves them); otherwise keep the hash in marin/harbor/iris_environment.py.
- Add an intermittent stress canary measuring sandbox scheduling latency, environment-ready time, and exec round-trip (mean and tail), so any saturation-aware admission policy is grounded in measured data.

Blocked on an operator decision: Cloud Build service account (builds.editor plus AR write for the eval parent's identity) and billing.

Done when:

- A full OpenThoughts-TBLite run performs no in-trial docker builds; images build once globally and are pulled by trials on docker-worker and k8s backends.
- The stress canary runs on a schedule and reports scheduling-latency, environment-ready, and exec round-trip percentiles.

topics.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
topics.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores: one
Zephyr task per normalized shard on GPU workers, tokenizing the text through the
tokenize stage's own core and reading the Harrier embedding by position. The Nemotron
tokenize leaves the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's
scores are registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than
rescored; a rerun of the score stage lands at the step's own identity. The
content-type leaves written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard, so a leaf from a
different normalize run fails its shard. `QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is
removed; the stage report reads its spot-check text from the normalized shard of
the same basename.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `QualityPin` carries
separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file, checked by the
worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed dataset without
moving or rescoring the raw scores. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores, and the calibration file parses into a `Calibration`
dataclass.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage run from text against the
same embeddings matched the pinned scores to a maximum difference of 1.6e-3 (mean
2.3e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a 4,096-document batch against the
earlier 32,768.

topics.title: [infra] Finish the fork-migration rollout and per-fork follow-ups
topics.body:
The weekly fork-migration system from #8048 is in place: a refresh-fork skill and
per-fork descriptors (#8068, #8117), a weekly ferry coordinator (#8245) with Loom
federation (#8284), and automated re-pinning for the vLLM GPU wheel (#8292). The TPU
vLLM stack refreshed to tpu-inference v0.26.0 (#8207) on top of the externalized
stack (#8063), and the GPU wheel now discovers its `_C` extension by shape across the
CUDA 13 / stable-ABI boundary (#8250). This issue tracks the work that remains after
that rollout, and is the canonical fork-migration tracker going forward. It supersedes
#8048 and folds in the refresh trackers #8298, #7097, #7143, and #6480.

1. Promote the Harbor one-time catch-up. marin-community/harbor#73 re-ports the fork
   overlay onto current upstream and folds the standalone `harbor-config` package into
   `harbor.models`. It is mergeable with `marin-precommit`, `marin-style-sync`, and
   `tests` green. Two steps need an admin/reviewer: drop the retired `harbor-config`
   context from the fork `main` branch protection (it no longer reports, so it blocks
   the merge), then review and merge, and promote the caught-up tree to protected
   `main`. Done when fork `main` carries the caught-up overlay and its protection no
   longer requires `harbor-config`.

2. Bump the Marin Harbor pin. After harbor#73 lands, re-pin `config/external/harbor`
   to the landed `main` SHA, migrate the `harbor_config.*` imports in
   `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py` to `harbor.models.*`, and
   keep the migration.toml [harbor] nuances. The aime-smoke e2e already passed
   end-to-end against the catch-up branch on qwen3-0.6b. Closes out the blocker path
   #8298.

topics.title: Pre-registering Snowball post-distillation SWE-bench pass@1
topics.body: Our aim is to predict the SWE-bench pass@1 of the final Snowball 9.97T base model after distilling on 2B tokens of SWE-smith trajectories generated by Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. We take the Snowball 3k, 9k, 18k, and 39k [intermediate checkpoints](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/snowball-intermediate) and [Grug](https://huggingface.co/penfever/grug-67b-a2b-sft-s1-wildchat-step257), and SFT them on [2B tokens](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nanoswe/swesmith-qwen3.6-35b-a3b) generated by a lightly fine-tuned variant of [Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/nanoswe/qwen-3.6-35b-a3b-teacher) against the [SWE-smith](https://huggingface.co/datasets/SWE-bench/SWE-smith) problem set. We SFT the Snowball checkpoints at 0.21B and 0.64B token budgets, and Grug additionally at 0.37B, 1.1B, and 1.9B budgets. We evaluate the bpb of all fine-tunes on 1.3k SWE-smith trajectories generated by the teacher model. We also evaluate the pass@1 of the Grug fine-tunes. We fit two scaling laws, one relating pre-training steps and SFT budget to bpb, and a second relating bpb to pass@1. We obtain a final prediction of 33% pass@1 for the 9.97T Snowball checkpoint fine-tuned on our SFT dataset. ## Predicting bpb on teacher trajectories We use a multiplicative law. In ongoing work using pre-training checkpoints trained under constant LR (SmolLM3), we found the following law to work well: ```math \text{bpb} = E \left(1 + A\, D_{\text{pre}}^{-\alpha}\right) \left(1 + B\, D_{\text{sft}}^{-\beta}\right) ``` To account for the LR schedule of Snowball, we use the approach of [Scaling Law with Learning Rate Annealing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11029) to model both the Grug anneal and the Snowball anneal. We thus turn $`1 + A\, D_{\text{pre}}^{-\alpha}`$ into ```math 1 + A\, S_1^{-\alpha} - C\, S_2 ``` where $`S_1 = 10^{-4} \sum_i \eta_i / \eta_{\text{peak}}`$ is the LR area over pre-training optimizer steps (proportional to $`D_{\text{pre}}`$ at constant LR, warmup counted at peak), and $`S_2 = 10^{-3} \sum_i m_i`$ is the annealing area, with momentum $`m_i = \lambda\, m_{i-1} + (\eta_{i-1} - \eta_i) / \eta_{\text{peak}}`$, $`\lambda = 0.999`$ (as in Tissue et al.), and $`\eta_{\text{peak}} = 5.28 \times 10^{-3}`$. The full law is ```math \text{bpb} = E \left(1 + A\, S_1^{-\alpha} - C\, S_2\right) \left(1 + B\, D_{\text{sft}}^{-\beta}\right) ``` with $`D_{\text{sft}}`$ in billions of tokens. We fit the six coefficients on our 13 datapoints using least squares, obtaining $`E = 0.0538,\ A = 0.278,\ \alpha = 0.783,\ C = 0.124,\ B = 0.260,\ \beta = 0.306`$, and a df-adjusted RMSE of 0.000441 bpb. Extrapolating to 9.97T pre-training tokens at 1.93B SFT tokens, we predict 0.0635 bpb. It is unclear whether calibrating the law on the much shorter Grug cooldown will extrapolate to the cooldown of Snowball. ## From bpb to pass@1 We fit the following law: ```math \log \text{pass@1} = a - b \cdot \text{bpb} ``` We fit the law using OLS on the five Grug SFTs, obtaining $`a = 5.98`$ and $`b = 39.1`$ (i.e., $`\text{pass@1} = 397\, e^{-39.1 \cdot \text{bpb}}`$), and extrapolate to the bpb predicted by the previous law, resulting in a predicted pass@1 of 33%. The 95% CI on the mean at the forecast is large: 29.3% to 37.5% pass@1. Our hunch is that the 33% prediction might be slightly conservative: fitting the law on only the three largest SFT budgets instead predicts 35%. ## Conclusion Our laws predict that fine-tuning the final Snowball checkpoint on our 2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B dataset will result in a SWE-bench pass@1 of **33%**. If anything we expect to err low, and would not be surprised by 35%.

comments.body:
**Update (Lightning SFT data).** We now fine-tune on SWE-smith trajectories generated by Nemotron 3.5 Lightning instead of Qwen 3.6. This is a separate prediction from the 33% above, which used Qwen 3.6 data and a different eval harness. We pre-register a new prediction for the final Snowball base model, as released by Marin, fine-tuned on **7.55B Lightning tokens** with the recipe of our Grug Lightning ladder (3,600 steps, 32k context). We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (483 instances, 5 attempts each).

![Snowball Lightning forecast](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rdolmedo/2ad458a02acae99b551f3739fa16834c/raw/e68176824598a2884c5b4fa02689f56094e3f0ac/forecast.png)

**Loss.** We predict **0.1334 bpb** on held-out Lightning trajectories. We start from Grug's measured Lightning loss at the same budget and subtract the Snowball–Grug gap predicted by the law above. To convert that gap from Qwen 3.6 loss to Lightning loss, we use the teacher map fitted at matched budgets on four students (SmolLM3 base, SmolLM3 mid-trained, Qwen3-4B, Grug):

```math
L_{\text{Lightning}} = 1.711\, L_{\text{Qwen 3.6}} + 0.033
```

We apply only its slope to the gap: $`\Delta L_{\text{Lightning}} = 1.711\, \Delta L_{\text{Qwen 3.6}}`$.

**pass@1.** We use three links. Each maps loss $`L`$ to ability $`\theta`$, and $`\theta`$ to pass@1 through a Rasch model averaged over the 483 instances, $`\text{pass@1} = \frac{1}{483}\sum_i \sigma(\theta - z_i)`$. Link 1 uses the instance difficulties $`z_i`$ fitted on the 29-model sweep; links 2 and 3 share difficulties fitted on the 25 Lightning fine-tunes.

| Link | $`\theta(L)`$ | pass@1 |
|---|---|---|
| Global ability law | $`13.22 - 47.59\,L`$ | **41.6%** |
| One law across four students on Lightning (SmolLM3 base/mid, Qwen3-4B, Grug) | $`10.94 - 68.17\,(1 - r\,e^{-D/D_0})\,L`$, with Grug's $`r = 0.065`$, $`D_0 = 4.57\text{B}`$ | **40.3%** |
| Grug only (linear) | $`8.39 - 48.98\,L`$ | **39.4%** |

We expect the law across four students to be the most accurate, which gives a final predicted pass@1 of **40.3%**.

We also pre-register each link as a function of the measured loss (middle panel), so the links can be checked even if the loss prediction misses.

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.

topics.title: Support context parallelism in the Hero pipeline
topics.body:
Add context parallelism to the Hero pipeline mesh, shard attention metadata with query tokens, and form next-token labels before sharding so a context slice can target the first token in the next slice. The smoke runner accepts a context-axis size and calculates batch divisibility without counting context replicas. Update the pipeline environment to CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2, Flash Attention 4 beta 28 or later, and Quack 0.6.4 for SM90 backward.

This draft targets a dependency-only integration branch combining #9119, #9282, and #9279 (which includes #9278). Its five-file diff contains the CP adaptation and dependency update; the prerequisite implementations remain in their existing PRs.

The full 535B, 48-layer model completed ten updates with finite losses on 192 H100s with PP24 × EP4 × CP2, 65,536-token sequences, global batch 96, and 24 microbatches: 6,291,456 tokens per update. Median step time was 68.539 seconds and measured MFU was 9.877%; loss went from 11.792197 to 11.449181. All 24 workers exited successfully. Gate 06 launched c55ab40a29 with exact helper dependency overrides; 3ad8d3ce37 subsequently recorded those dependencies. Runtime and dependency files match 3ad8d3ce37; a later test-only fix compares discontinuous histogram router statistics at matching per-layer execution boundaries. Detailed results are in #9277.

The run still required scratch JAXPP overlays for host-memory mesh rebinding, forward activation-offload placement, and the Dime2 send-buffer lifetime backport. It also retained disposable warmup, host parking of model state, and CUDA synchronization after each step. The required overlays block a stock-install recipe, and the root cause behind the retained synchronization workaround remains unresolved. This is a bounded synthetic-data stepping result.

The integration passed the safe suite with 1,929 tests passed, 5 skipped, and 5 expected failures. After the histogram test fix, all eight affected pipeline tests passed, including the two-CPU CP2-versus-CP1 loss and all-gradient regression. Tolerances are unchanged. Scoped lint passed.

The stable fork has **68 non-merge overlay commits** across **113 paths**; upstream also changed **47** of those paths. The [stable overlay](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/compare/9d88ceb02694c6e3df182ec3c87201284f50e2c6...1c020822a8878b540c16672915216d3263f82406) and [upstream advance](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/9d88ceb02694c6e3df182ec3c87201284f50e2c6...c599b5971faf7ed8bff4bd1b14713293c20082d6) are the replay inputs.

Marin still pins release [`marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac), source `01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e`. It does not contain the current stable overlay and was left unchanged. No new staging ref or rollback/date tag was created; no wheel build, GPU qualification, Snowball parity test, or Marin adoption PR ran.

The current upstream tip has not been replayed: the refresh playbook routes overlays hundreds of commits behind upstream to a one-time manual catch-up, including a carry/drop/fix audit of the real commits. 🤖 2026-10-12 refresh audit: selected upstream `main` at [`6e6e86078afe73af5180a9888e88751d51ef1b31`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/6e6e86078afe73af5180a9888e88751d51ef1b31). Protected fork `main` remains [`1c020822a8878b540c16672915216d3263f82406`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/1c020822a8878b540c16672915216d3263f82406), based on upstream `9d88ceb02694c6e3df182ec3c87201284f50e2c6`. The new base is 1,708 upstream commits beyond that base; the stable overlay has 68 non-merge commits across 113 paths. Marin still pins GPU release `marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac`, source `01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e`.

A local replay applied the TPU dependency, CMake cleanup, and metadata commits. The old Grug scheduler guard in `dabaa7a7484f` targets routing state upstream moved into `AuxOutputConnector`, while its `setup.py` fallback hardcodes version `0.20.1rc1`; this commit needs a fresh carry/drop decision. The next three commits applied, then `881e2d46fa2b` conflicted in four upstream-shared files: `requirements/common.txt`, `tests/models/registry.py`, `vllm/transformers_utils/config.py`, and `vllm/transformers_utils/configs/__init__.py`. This is a manual GrugMoE API port across core model/configuration files, not a fork-new file cascade. The scratch replay stopped there; it supplies no reviewed `main-next` tip or fork test result.

Remote `main-next` remains `47b411d5785d1c3dee0328334472d70310c53feb` from the older candidate. No new remote branch, rollback/date tags, GPU wheel build, H100/GB200 qualification, Snowball parity test, or Marin adoption PR resulted from this audit. A one-time manual catch-up must replay the real overlay commits, audit the CUDA/Torch and `vllm._C_stable_libtorch` boundary, and produce a reviewed tip. An admin then promotes that tip to protected `main` before the GPU wheel workflow runs. The TPU 0.31 pair also waits on this source path; [its blocker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9751) records the missing AuxOutput API on current fork `main`.

topics.title: [grug] Add the Hero-mix and quality-classifier fast tracks
topics.body:
* add two data fast tracks next to the model ladder. all three tracks train the same dense/MoE ladder (d512–d1280) on 8×H100 and compare on final Paloma macro loss
* model ladder: `fast-track` trains on the frozen `hero_tok/v16384_shuf/train` cache, as before
  * `launch.py` resolves the budget in `resolve_h100_ladder_budget` and takes a `TrainingSource`, so the data tracks use the same training wiring
  * add `--seed` and `--data-seed`. `--submit` forwards `WANDB_MODE` and accepts `WANDB_MODE=disabled` without `WANDB_API_KEY`
* hero mix plus a new dataset: sample the production Hero mixture and give a new Hugging Face dataset a fraction `p` of the training tokens
  * `hero_sample_cli` replays `harrier_mix_2026_08_18.json` over `store_4d2e363d` in the production loader order and retokenizes each source segment as BOS + text + EOS with `hero-bpe-v16384` into a `PreparedHeroSample`. build it once at the largest ladder budget (17,478,713,344 tokens) and use it again for all rungs
  * `add_dataset_cli` tokenizes a bounded HF prefix at an immutable revision, scales the Hero weights by `1 - p`, and caps the new data at `C = min(p·B, (N/T)·B)` to simulate the production epoch count [^1]
  * `hero_baseline_cli` trains the matched control on the same `PreparedHeroSample`
  * the Hero cell capacity check runs on the final mixture weights, so a small `p` cannot make the largest cell repeat its data
* quality classifier: sample raw text from all 292 registered sources in proportion to corpus size, score it with a frozen head, and train on the top documents
  * `corpus_sample_cli` builds a `RawCorpusPool` with `corpus-id-interval-v1`: one seeded cyclic interval in the 128-bit document-ID space for each source. it skips a row group only when its ID statistics show no overlap. `--label-exclusion-manifest` is required
  * `quality_labels_cli` freezes the GLM-5.2 labels and fits a ridge head on cached Harrier features (target `(quality - 1) / 4`, 80/10/10 split by duplicate group). the raw pool excludes all labelled duplicate groups
  * `quality_cli --stage features|score|select|train` scores the pool once at the largest rung. for budget `B`, it ranks the first `10·B` raw tokens and keeps whole documents until they fill `B`. `--selection-method candidate|incumbent|random` gives the matched controls
* the data-track CLIs default to MoE and derive `--data-seed` from `--seed`, the same as `fast-track`
* add `fast-track-long-string-v1` for HF and raw-corpus tokenization: split at the first whitespace at or after 10,000 characters, and reject a document above 64 MiB with its source and ID
  * bound native tokenizer batches by bytes. a local 32 MiB probe kept all 19,532,169 token IDs, and peak RSS went from 4.60 GiB to 2.85 GiB
* rename `max_train_batches` → `max_train_sequences` in `LmDataConfig`, so a component cap does not depend on the batch size
* fixes found during the runs
  * iris: repair missing CUDA toolchain files. put the child job and attempt in JAX coordinator names, because sibling training jobs connected to the coordinator of a different job
  * fray: pass actor concurrency to Iris RPC servers, because the 32-thread default let long waits block worker heartbeats. the inference broker sets its concurrency explicitly
  * datakit CPU drivers install the `cpu` group with `datakit`, so that they do not resolve the CUDA Torch wheel
  * artifact loading keeps absolute bucket paths, grug dispatch forwards `WANDB_MODE`, and levanter keeps eval metrics between detail intervals
* results at this time (seed 0, final macro loss from the training logs [^2])
  * hero mix, MoE, change against the Hero baseline at the same rung [^3]:

    | rung | 10% Paloma | 10% Uncheatable | 99% Paloma | 99% Uncheatable |
    |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
    | d512 | +4.22% | +1.95% | +58.70% | +68.40% |
    | d768 | +3.30% | +1.56% | +56.97% | +63.72% |
    | d1024 | +4.28% | +1.51% | +55.47% | +61.68% |
    | d1280 | not valid | not valid | +48.85% | +60.26% |

  * each valid mixed run is worse on all 23 evaluation datasets. for 10% at d512 dense, three matched seeds changed Paloma loss by +0.05%, +0.05%, and −0.14%
  * quality, four-source pilot (`cp/arxiv_abstracts`, `cp/wikiteam`, `docx-corpus/en`, `starcoder2/documentation`, 6,064,023 documents): ridge selection against random selection gave Paloma macro BPB 1.9051 against 1.6164, and 20 of 23 datasets were worse
  * these probes test the mechanics. they use assumed production counts and one seed, so they do not show the value of WikiText or of the ridge head
* open work
  * build the `resample-v2` Hero sample and run the four-scale Hero-mix comparison again on it
  * the all-292 raw pool stopped after about 14 h: `stack-v3` has documents of 79–213 MB, above the 64 MiB limit. a policy is necessary (drop and count, raise the limit, or exclude the source). no four-scale quality run exists yet
  * the 10% d1280 run resumed from a temporary checkpoint after a preemption near step 14.1k. its training loss went from 1.45 to 2.75 and did not recover, so the result is not valid. the cause is not known
  * training reads the new dataset in HF prefix order, because the Hero mixture uses `shuffle=False` and Levanter has no shuffle for one component
  * the pool excludes only the candidate's labels, not the training labels of an incumbent scorer
* remove the DataKit end-to-end track from this PR [^4]

[^1]: `N` is the number of available unique tokens in the new dataset, `T` is the production budget (default 18.75T), and `B` is the rung budget. the loader cap rounds down to whole sequences.
[^2]: these runs used W&B offline mode, so the values come from the `levanter.eval` log lines.
[^3]: these runs used the earlier resampler, which kept the source BOS as text and did not put an EOS after the last segment of a source example. the control and the treatment used the same sample, so each delta compares like with like, but the sample differs from `resample-v2`. old `PreparedHeroSample` and `PreparedAddDatasetCache` artifacts must be prepared again.
[^4]: this removes `--source-mode sample|registry`, the token-shuffle control, the shared Zephyr pool (`execution_scope`), and coordinator driver placement in the reference DataKit pipeline. the 25B-sample results and controls are in an earlier revision of this description.

topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids

Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. topics.title: [eval] Check in the September evaluation campaign
topics.body:
Check in the model, evaluator, and launcher configurations for the September 2026 evaluation campaign, together with the runtime fixes needed for serving, retry, resume, and coverage. The launcher validates external pins, writes immutable effective-config snapshots, and accepts an optional submitter-controlled version label. That label does not attest policy conformance.

Harbor results are bound to the full model and hosted judge configurations, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit. Resume checks this identity before submission and reuse. A changed checkpoint under the same served name is rejected, as are existing roots without model-bound provenance. Recovery retries known infrastructure failures and unscored trials while retaining scored outcomes and unknown errors.

The frozen Harbor runtime pins 94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe and includes the Tau3 adapter. The Evalchemy lock and generated pin match Marin's external dependency configuration.

SWE-bench uses the native Mini-SWE adapter from merged [Harbor #232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) and [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233). Its 32,768-token context includes the prompt and reply together. Mini-SWE counts the rendered prompt through the serving tokenizer, including tools and the generation prefix, and caps the reply within the remaining budget and server window. Harbor loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before applying overrides and selects its batch agent, which saves the trajectory on context exhaustion without prompting. Harbor can then verify the existing patch.

Sotopia uses the packaged agent from merged [Harbor #231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231). Judge failures become verifier infrastructure errors. The Marin agent wrappers and their harness dependencies are removed. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget, so those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy.

Part of #9566.

topics.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
topics.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

topics.title: [ferries] Document bisecting a TPU canary MFU change
topics.body:
A scheduled canary run narrows an MFU change only to the commits between two runs, usually 9 to 16 a day. A new section in `experiments/ferries/OPS.md` re-runs the canary configuration at commits in that range: list the commits that touch training code, submit the middle one straight to Iris at batch priority from a worktree of that commit, compare its median MFU and tokens/s with the scheduled runs either side, and repeat. The `run-ferries` skill points at the section. The existing datakit content moves under its own heading, unchanged.

The procedure is the one used on 2026-10-02 to bisect the 2026-09-09 TPU canary drop from 0.661% to 0.609% MFU. Three runs at `20d35b9019`, `770b675fbf` and `5bd45c5ae8` each measured 0.663%, which puts the drop on #8960 (`efe7989206`). The section records three constraints found along the way:

- Dispatching the canary workflow with `gh workflow run` joins its `canary-ferry` concurrency group, which has `cancel-in-progress: true`, so a bisection run would cancel the scheduled canary or be cancelled by it. Runs go to Iris directly at `--priority batch`, and the TPU training child inherits that band.
- The controller rejects a root submission from an `iris` client more than 14 days older than itself, which rules out the CLI at the tested commit. The commands use the current checkout's CLI while bundling the old commit's code; child jobs are not checked.
- Iris forwards `WANDB_API_KEY` and `HF_TOKEN` only from the submitting shell, so the commands export them from local credential files.

Only the TPU canary is covered. The H100 path through the `iris-ci` controller is untested.

topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:

The `tpu-vllm` refresh to upstream tpu-inference `v0.30.0` cannot pass the exact-pair runtime gate.
