topics.title: [zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails
topics.body:
When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__` sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed, and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so `atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

topics.title: [levanter] Stop background iterators after completion
topics.body:
Buffered background iterators now remain stopped after the producer finishes or raises. Previously, consuming the single end marker or error left later `next()` calls waiting forever on an empty queue. Levanter uses this iterator to prefetch data loader batches and evaluation requests.

Regression tests reproduce the hang after normal exhaustion and producer failure in bounded and unbounded queues. The affected safe suite passed 1,063 tests with 13 skips.

topics.title: [haliax] Prefer XLA ragged_dot on AMD MI300X and MI325X
topics.body:
On AMD MI300X and MI325X (gfx942), `ragged_dot(implementation="auto")` now tries XLA before the Pallas Triton kernels. MI350X (gfx950), NVIDIA, TPU and CPU keep their current order. `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` still overrides the choice.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X found that XLA's bf16 grouped GEMM takes 11-28% less time than the best Triton config for each fwd, dlhs and drhs triple. For example, the June w13 projection at M=131072 took 10.91 ms with XLA and 12.25 ms with tuned Triton. These numbers come from microbenchmarks only. We have not run a full-model A/B on MI300X. MI350X must keep Triton because XLA rejects bf16 `ragged_dot` on gfx950.

XLA's hipBLASLt grouped GEMM crashes with `ROCM_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` when HIP command buffers are on, so ROCm runs must pass `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`. The MI300X timings above used that flag. The Grug training entry points already set it by default, and so does the HPC Fund Slurm wrapper, `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` on `main`.

`_GpuFamily` gains an `AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` member, detected from the compute capability that ROCm reports (`"gfx942"`). gfx942 keeps the tile-map kernels and the block configs swept on MI350X, so the Triton fallback is unchanged. #9905 is stacked on this PR and reuses `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` for its MI300X block configs, so merge #10009, then this PR, then #9905.

At #9905's head, which contains this PR, the file gives 46 passed and 30 skipped f32 kernel cases on MI300X (job 458222) and 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223).

Stacked on #10009. Merge #10009 first, then retarget this PR to `main`.

topics.title: [haliax] Tune tile-map ragged_dot dlhs and drhs blocks for MI300X
topics.body:
Give MI300X and MI325X (gfx942) their own dlhs and drhs tile-map blocks for the Triton `ragged_dot` kernels: 128x256x32, 4 warps, 8 XCDs, group_m=2, with 2 pipeline stages for dlhs and 1 for drhs. Until now gfx942 reused the MI350X (gfx950) blocks. gfx942 has 64 KiB of LDS per CU, against 160 KiB on gfx950, and the MI350X dlhs and drhs blocks run 20-35% slower on MI300X than the swept tile. The forward pass keeps the MI350X block (256x256x64). 128x256x32 is 16% faster for fwd at the June shape with M=16384, but no faster at M=131072 and 15-22% slower at a Mixtral-like shape.

The table is keyed on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` from #9904. That PR makes `implementation="auto"` prefer XLA on gfx942, so these blocks apply when Triton is selected explicitly. Merge order: #10009, then #9904, then this PR.

The f32 skip in `test_triton_kernel_families_match_ragged_dot_general`, which #10009 adds for gfx942, now keys on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942`. Triton uses xf32 for f32 dots on gfx942, and the group-grid f32 tiles exceed the 64 KiB LDS.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X (partition `mi3001x`; jobs 454650, 454673, 454679 and 454683; sweeps 454658, 454659, 454667 and 454668) show that the tuned dlhs and drhs blocks cut a fwd+dlhs+drhs triple by 9-24%. For example, the June w13 shape at M=131072 drops from 14.67 ms to 12.25 ms.

At this branch's head, `lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py` gives 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223) and, on MI300X, 46 passed and 30 skipped (job 458222).

Part of #9812

topics.title: [post-training] Compare SFT, rejection-sampled SFT and OPD transfer on Snowball with CruxEval
topics.body:
Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LVfMDHRBKBk_Bn9PY1J9Lb_MYwdUTFP5PkX2br25TNg/edit?tab=t.izhzsywzorld. Final results and the full ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 (ledger also at https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0).

**TL;DR (final, 2026-10-09).** Given one expert E built from the Snowball student B by SFT on GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces, three methods were used to transfer E's gain back into B: plain SFT on E's traces, SFT on rejection-sampled E traces (RS-SFT), and on-policy distillation from E (OPD). All three recover most or all of E's CruxEval gain on the 1,600 training-is-test prompts. Two-pass CruxEval input / output accuracy on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0, RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9, OPD 79.6 / 75.2, against E 79.4 / 71.4 and B 55.4 / 57.8. RS-SFT and OPD are both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering (1.2 / 2.7 pp) is unresolved with one run per arm and two evaluator passes. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K or MATH500. Training cost: plain SFT 61.6 H100-h, RS-SFT 57.4, OPD 376.4 for the full run (286.9 to the selected checkpoint, plus 14–15 per HF export). RS-SFT used ground-truth execution results to select demos; the other arms did not. These numbers measure transfer on seen prompts, not generalization.

**Results (selected checkpoints; CruxEval two-pass means, pass@1 %, 800 problems per direction; "gap closed" = gain over B divided by E's gain over B).**

| Model | CruxEval input | CruxEval output | Gap closed (in / out) | GSM8K | MATH500 | Training H100-h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B (student) | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 | — |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — | — |
| E (expert; B + SFT on GLM traces, step 272) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 | 35.9 |
| Plain SFT on E demos, 400 updates (final) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 | 61.6 |
| RS-SFT on execution-correct E demos, 283 of 376 updates | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 | 57.4 (full run) |
| OPD from E, 75 of 100 updates | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 | 286.9 to the checkpoint; 376.4 full run; +14–15 per HF export |

**Models.** Student B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`. E = B after full SFT on 1,454 execution-correct GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 272 updates, 32 H100, fresh optimizer state, frozen router biases), export `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`. E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. E+ (E + 2 epochs at LR 1e-6; 80.2 / 75.1) was built as a separate reference and is not an arm. Every arm starts from B.

**Benchmark.** CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped as the target because B already scores 89.8% there; GSM8K and MATH500 are the collapse checks. Teacher gate: B 55.4 / 57.8; GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts 94.0 / 90.5; E 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean), passing the gate of B + 10 points on both tasks with no GSM8K drop.

**Frozen evaluator.** Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8` (corrected 2026-10-13: the revision that actually ran is `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`, recorded in every record's `eval_runtime` field; `c131e5ab` was the code constant in `eval_policy.py`, which the launcher did not use. The scorer and sampling settings are the ones at ae362881 throughout, so no number changes.), vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). One pass on 800 problems has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp; selected checkpoints get two passes.

**Arms as run (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the 1,600 prompts; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- E demos: 8 samples per prompt from E at temperature 1.0, both directions, execution-graded in an isolated container (12,800 samples, 14.6 H100-h, shared by both SFT arms).
- Plain SFT: E's first sample per prompt, correct or not (1,600 rows; 1.45M supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16; Levanter, 32 H100).
- RS-SFT: first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows; 97 prompts with no correct sample stay in the eval denominator; 1.06M supervised tokens per epoch; Levanter, 32 H100).
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, 4 on-policy rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E as the teacher (sampled reverse KL on chosen tokens, no verifier), 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch; 4 learner + 1 rollout + 1 teacher H100x8 nodes (Megatron).
- Selection: the final checkpoint when it is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions, otherwise a second pass on both and the two-pass means decide. Plain SFT selected its final checkpoint (400 updates); RS-SFT (283 of 376) and OPD (75 of 100) selected their epoch-3 checkpoints after their finals dropped on one direction.

**Artifacts.** Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces, side-by-side compare): https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. OPD W&B: marin-community/skyrl run p3ie2bg7. Selected exports: plain `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`, RS-SFT `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`, OPD `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`. Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/<record>/record.json`.

**Not in scope.** Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval).

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher.
- 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used.
- 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain.
- 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm.
- 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris.
- 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. Final results posted in one comment; the running-log comments were removed and are archived with the ledger.

comments.body:
🤖 Final results: SFT vs rejection-sampled SFT vs on-policy distillation for transferring the CruxEval expert back into B

TL;DR. All three arms recover most or all of the expert's CruxEval gain. Every arm trains on prompts drawn from the same 1,600 the evaluator scores (800 input-prediction and 800 output-prediction problems; plain SFT and OPD use all 1,600, RS-SFT the 1,503 with an execution-correct E sample), so this is transfer on seen prompts. Two-pass means on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0 (400 updates), RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9 (283 updates), OPD 79.6 / 75.2 (75 updates); the expert E scores 79.4 / 71.4 and B scores 55.4 / 57.8 (CruxEval input / output, pass@1 on 800 problems each). RS-SFT's two-pass means are 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD's; two passes on one run per arm do not resolve that ordering. Both are above plain SFT by 5.7–6.9 pp on input and 3.2–5.9 pp on output. Training cost: OPD 287 H100-h from allocation to the selected checkpoint (376 for the full 4-epoch run); plain SFT 62 and RS-SFT 57 for their full 4-epoch runs (the RS candidate is update 283 of 376 and was not timed separately). RS-SFT also used ground-truth execution results to pick its demos, which the other arms did not have. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K (B 90.4) or MATH500 (B 89.8); OPD 75 scores 90.4 on MATH500, 1.8 below E, inside MATH500's binomial 95% half-width of about 2.6 pp at n=500. These numbers do not measure generalization to unseen prompts.

Setup (the design doc is linked from the issue body).

- Student B: `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`.
- Expert E: B after full SFT on 1,454 GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, step 272 (35.9 H100-h). E+ (E + 2 epochs at 1e-6, 80.2 / 75.1) is a reference only.
- Evaluator: Evalchemy ae362881 (corrected 2026-10-13: the revision that actually ran is `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`, recorded in every record's `eval_runtime` field; `c131e5ab` was the code constant in `eval_policy.py`, which the launcher did not use. The scorer and sampling settings are the ones at ae362881 throughout, so no number changes.), vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking enabled, unseeded sampling at vLLM's default temperature 1.0 (the lm-eval chat client sends no sampling parameters). One pass has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp at n=800 (p≈0.55) and 3.0 pp at p≈0.75. Paired deltas use a problem-resampling bootstrap conditional on the sampled completions. Gist of all evaluator configs: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71.
- Matched AdamW hyperparameters across arms, in different implementations (Levanter for the SFT arms, Megatron for OPD): LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen (E froze it too; all exports verified to carry B's 26 router-bias tensors).
- Plain SFT: B + 4 epochs on E's first sample per prompt (1,600 rows, unfiltered), batch 16, 32 H100. 1,452,363 supervised tokens per epoch.
- RS-SFT: all 12,800 E samples (k=8) execution-graded in an isolated container; first correct sample per prompt kept. 1,503 of 1,600 prompts covered (774 input / 729 output); the 97 uncovered prompts stay in the eval denominator. 4 epochs, 376 updates. 1,056,479 supervised tokens per epoch.
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, B samples 4 rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E scores them (sampled reverse KL on the chosen tokens, coefficient 1.0, reward replaced by the distillation signal, no verifier). 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch, 4 epochs. 4 learner nodes (PP2 × EP8) + 1 rollout node + 1 teacher node, all H100x8.
- Selection procedure used (the rule 'prefer the final checkpoint when similar or better on both directions' was agreed before the final checkpoints were scored; the operational reading of similar as 'paired 95% CI includes 0' was fixed while applying it): if the final checkpoint is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions on the first pass, select it; otherwise run a second pass on both checkpoints and choose on the two-pass means. GSM8K and MATH500 run on the selected checkpoint and on any terminal checkpoint that lost the selection.

Results. CruxEval pass@1 (%), input / output. "Gap closed" is the gain over B divided by E's two-pass gain over B (24.06 pp input, 13.63 pp output). GSM8K (flexible-extract, 0-shot) and MATH500 are single pass for every model.

| Model | Input | Output | Gap closed | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 |
| E (CruxEval 2-pass mean) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT, 400 updates (2-pass mean) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 |
| RS-SFT, 283 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 |
| OPD, 75 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 |

Learning curves (single pass per checkpoint; the training trajectory, not the selection basis):

| Arm | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 | Epoch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain SFT (101/201/301/400 updates) | 69.6 / 67.5 | 73.5 / 69.9 | 69.4 / 71.8 | 74.8 / 71.3 |
| RS-SFT (95/189/283/376 updates) | 75.5 / 72.0 | 82.0 / 75.8 | 81.4 / 77.1 | 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD (25/50/75/100 updates) | 74.9 / 68.9 | 81.8 / 75.8 | 79.0 / 76.8 | 80.9 / 72.3 |

Selection. Plain SFT's final checkpoint was similar or better than its epoch-3 checkpoint on both directions (+5.4 / −0.5 pp), so it was selected and repeated (second pass 73.1 / 72.8). RS-SFT's final checkpoint was 4.4 pp below epoch 3 on input, and OPD's final checkpoint was 4.5 pp below epoch 3 on output, each with a paired CI excluding 0. Both arms got a second pass on their last two checkpoints. RS-SFT: 376 updates 76.1 / 76.2 against 283 updates 80.8 / 77.9 (two-pass means); the final is lower on both directions, so 283 was selected. OPD: 100 updates 79.875 / 72.0 against 75 updates 79.625 / 75.19; input differs by 0.25 pp and the final is 3.19 pp lower on output, so 75 was selected. The terminal checkpoints are reported in the curve table, not as the method result. The second passes reuse the same runs, so the four pass pairings per arm are one comparison, not four. Same-checkpoint pass pairs moved by up to 3.1 pp (OPD 75 output: 76.75 on pass 1, 73.6 on pass 2, paired CI [−6.0, −0.25]), so the conditional problem-bootstrap intervals do not capture all generation variability; two repeats are too few to estimate it. The final-checkpoint drops are therefore suggestive, not established.

Paired comparisons at the selected checkpoints (pass 1 vs pass 1; 95% bootstrap CI): RS-SFT 283 vs OPD 75: +2.4 [−1.0, +5.8] input / +0.4 [−2.5, +3.3] output on pass 1, and 0.0 [−3.4, +3.3] / +5.0 [+2.0, +8.0] on pass 2. RS-SFT 283 vs plain 400: +6.6 [+3.1, +10.1] / +5.9 [+2.8, +9.3] (pass 2: +7.1 / +5.9). OPD 75 vs plain 400: +4.3 [+0.9, +7.9] / +5.5 [+2.3, +8.8] (pass 2: +7.1 / +0.9 [−2.3, +4.0]). Against E (pass 1): RS-SFT 283 +2.0 [−1.5, +5.5] / +6.9 [+3.8, +10.1]; OPD 75 −0.4 [−3.8, +3.0] / +6.5 [+3.5, +9.5]; plain 400 −4.6 [−8.4, −1.0] / +1.0 [−2.4, +4.5]. Pass-1 and pass-2 pairings share the training runs; they are two draws of the evaluator, not two experiments.

Response shape: B leaves no final answer after the thinking block in 1,110 of 1,600 CruxEval responses; E in about 90. The same count was not made for the three arms, so part of each arm's gain may be this shape change. The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model. Correct/n on pass 1 and pass 2: B 1/26, 1/71; E 2/26, 1/71 and 1/26, 4/71; plain 400 0/26, 3/71 and 0/26, 4/71; RS-SFT 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71; OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71. The slice was selected by E failing all 8 samples on these prompts, so E's low score is selection-induced. RS-SFT saw no demos for these prompts. Comparing different methods on 97 selected prompts does not identify the effect of omitting them, so these are counts only.

Cost (H100-hours, Iris task-runtime accounting). Training figures are full-run costs for 4 epochs and include in-gang startup, native saves and exports; they exclude CPU preprocessing, demo generation and evals. The selected RS-SFT checkpoint is update 283 of 376 and the selected OPD checkpoint is update 75 of 100; costs are not pro-rated to the candidate. OPD's allocation-to-checkpoint figure comes from the run's log timestamps and ends at the checkpoint request, so it excludes the native save; plain SFT's 61.6 runs through its final HF export and job teardown. The two selected-cost endpoints are therefore not identical.

| Arm | Training (full 4-epoch run) | Demo generation | Exports | Allocation to selected checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E (expert) | 35.9 for 3 epochs (+15.3 in aborted attempts) | GLM traces via relay, no GPU-h on our side | in-gang | — |
| Plain SFT | 61.6 | shares the one k=8 E collection (14.6 measured once for all 12,800 demos, plus a 0.7 pilot; plain used 1 of the 8 samples, and no standalone 1-sample generation run was timed) | in-gang | 61.6 (final checkpoint selected) |
| RS-SFT | 57.4 | the same k=8 E collection (14.6, counted once for both SFT arms) + CPU execution grading | in-gang | full run 57.4; update 283 was not timed separately |
| OPD | 376.4 (6 nodes × 7h50m) | none (on-policy) | 58.8 (4 export-only jobs, 14–15 each) | 286.9 from allocation start to the update-75 checkpoint request (before the native save completes), plus its 14.2 export job |

OPD also spent 73.5 H100-h on smoke tests, debugging and the export path and 4.6 on a startup failure (missing W&B key) before the full run. These training-only figures are not the experiment total; the ledger adds evaluation (about 3.3 per CruxEval pass), failed-eval overhead, E and E+ training, and the reference runs. OPD per-update wall time was 4–5 min (256 sampled responses, 30,720-token cap) against about 17 s per SFT update; one prompt epoch is 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD and 1 demo for SFT, so epochs are matched on prompts, not on tokens or compute. One CruxEval pass costs about 3.3 H100-h; the ledger lists every eval run. Failed eval groups (serve preemption with a stale endpoint in the eval runner, and one preflight disconnect; see below) cost about 11 H100-h.

Confidence. The gains over B are large relative to noise (the lower 95% bound of every arm's paired gain over B is at least 9.8 pp). Between arms, the measured two-pass means put RS-SFT 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD and both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; each arm is one training run with no LR sweep, same-checkpoint pass pairs moved 0.5–3.1 pp on the six repeated checkpoints, and two repeats do not estimate run-to-run variance, so the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering is unresolved and the gap to plain SFT is the better-supported difference. The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

topics.title: [rl] Invalidate Atlas reviews for source-specific grading changes
topics.body:
Atlas previously invalidated a saved quality review when the shared verifier repository revision changed, including changes unrelated to that source. Fingerprint each MarinSkyRL source's selected grading code, prompts, runtime dependencies and task-owned verifier assets so unrelated repository edits preserve its grading identity.

Require an archived, hash-verified proof that a saved review covers the current dataset revision and grading identity. New task-verifier executions attest their grading inputs before publication. Historical reviews remain current when archived evidence establishes that the selected grading inputs or behavior are equivalent. Otherwise the source needs current quality review. Original reviews and their captured execution revisions remain available.

Harbor-backed Nemotron SWE identities include selected proxy verifier files, permissions, judge settings and grader environments. GenRM difficulty displays mean task-verifier rewards and bootstrap confidence intervals from 16-candidate comparison pools; it does not convert those rewards into solved-task counts.

Regression tests cover grading changes, unrelated code and documentation edits, selected task assets and invalid review proofs. The export preserves all 206 source IDs. The 103 MarinSkyRL sources have grading fingerprints; adding task assets changes the ten Harbor fingerprints and preserves the other 93. Task Trove sources retain their existing pinned dataset references. Type checking and required lint pass. After merging main at dcddd68f9b, the affected safe test run passes 2,623 tests with seven failures reproduced independently on that clean main commit. All 79 Atlas backend and grading-code tests pass, including a packaged-backend migration regression. All ten Harbor task-asset manifests match after the upstream archive helper move. The catalog is bundled as a Python string literal because Marina extracts only server Python files for backend execution. Public applet version 68 preserves all source IDs and pinned data references.

topics.title: [grug] Route QBRoutedMoE through the jax_triton top-k kernel
topics.body:
QBRoutedMoE now selects experts with `levanter.grug._moe.topk.top_k_indices`, called per token shard inside `shard_map`, in place of `jax.lax.top_k`. That is the jax_triton kernel from #9830, which the hero model already uses. `jax.lax.top_k` still handles rows of 1,024 or more (XLA:GPU runs its own top-k kernel on those), non-float32 inputs, non-GPU backends and environments without jax-triton.

On AMD, jax-triton 0.3.1 with triton 3.6.0, Levanter's GPU pins, compiles the kernel for ROCm with jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer. jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher, so there the kernel falls back to `jax.lax.top_k`.

Time per call in ms, from 16 calls on distinct inputs in one executable, median of 5 runs. The shapes are the router logits per call of the hero model and of the June Snowball model:

| shape, k | GPU | `lax.top_k` | jax_triton (this PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | GB200 | 0.837 | 0.0754 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | H100 | 1.107 | 0.0954 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI300X | 0.847 | 0.0665 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI350X | 1.000 | 0.0570 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | GB200 | 0.229 | 0.0207 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | H100 | 0.308 | 0.0238 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI300X | 0.351 | 0.0246 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI350X | 0.402 | 0.0167 |

The AMD rows ran on jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0, with the AMD HPC Fund cluster's ROCm 7.2 libraries on the library path, as `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` leaves them. The `lax.top_k` baseline depends on that: with only the wheel's own ROCm libraries loaded, `lax.top_k` on MI350X takes 2.4 ms (hero) and 1.7 ms (June), while the kernel times do not change. The kernel code is unchanged since #9830; the NVIDIA rows are earlier measurements of it with the same harness.

On NVIDIA, the models that use QBRoutedMoE (`experiments/grug/moe`, `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp` and `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe`) now run the kernel, because Levanter's GPU extra installs jax-triton. In the optimized HLO of the June training step on H100 and GB200, the 4 `sort` ops of main's routing become 2 `triton_kernel_call`s, and the all-gathers, all-reduces and reduce-scatters are unchanged. Step time does not change measurably. June model at full width with 4 layers and sequence length 4096, ring expert parallelism over the node, `xla_flash` attention and XLA `ragged_dot`; median of steps 2-19 per run, runs alternating between main and this PR:

| GPU | Tokens per GPU | Runs per side | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4x GB200 | 8,192 | 4 | 0.5742 s (0.5723-0.5759) | 0.5740 s (0.5719-0.5760) |
| 8x H100 | 16,384 | 5 | 1.457 s (1.403-1.508) | 1.513 s (1.336-1.539) |

On H100, step time varied between runs of the same code: main's five runs spanned 1.403-1.508 s (7%) and this PR's 1.336-1.539 s (15%). Five runs per side cannot separate the two. Scaled to these shapes, the per-call times above put the saving below 0.1% of a step. At 16,384 tokens per GPU on GB200, runs of both variants intermittently hung in a training step or ran out of memory, so those runs are left out. TPU step time was not measured; there `top_k_indices` falls back to `lax.top_k` inside the same `shard_map`.

On MI300X and MI350X the kernel's indices equal those of `lax.top_k` computed on the CPU, for widths 37 to 1,023 and k up to 37, on random, tied, constant, ±0, ±inf and NaN rows. ROCm's own `lax.top_k` ties -0 with +0 and orders NaN payloads differently, while the kernel follows XLA:CPU and CUDA. The GPU tests therefore check the kernel's output against `lax.top_k` run on the CPU backend.

The AMD venv recipe in `experiments/amd/hpcfund/README.md` still installs jaxlib 0.11.0 without jax-triton, so runs from it silently keep `lax.top_k` until that recipe moves to 0.11.1.

Supersedes #9889, which added a separate ROCm-only Pallas kernel for power-of-two widths.

topics.title: [grug] Let the hero launch use the carry-offload memory budget
topics.body:
`trigger_hero.sh` passed `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.75` and `--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor=85` to the hero coordinator. Since #9831, `_apply_hero_ep_runtime_defaults` gives the hero's carry-offload configuration a 0.78 memory fraction and slop factor 105 together with `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading`. Explicit values take precedence over those defaults, and `run_grug` copies the coordinator environment into the training tasks, so a hero launched from main would compile with 0.75 / 85 and host-memory offloading on. On one GB200 rack restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint, that combination aborts compilation on every rank in `HloRematerialization` (`hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118`, `Check failed: !place_before_list.empty()`).

Without the two overrides the launch resolves to 0.78 / 105 with host-memory offloading, the configuration measured in the #9831–#9834 rack benchmarks. The live hero is unaffected: Iris retries reuse the bundle it was launched with.

Follow-up to #9831.

topics.title: [eval] Iris retries overwrite completed run records
topics.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-nupa-9a91/results` held a sealed 5,000-item attempt with 2,414 correct answers (`0.4828`). Iris classified the completed Evalchemy child attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted`, retried the same task and path, and the final canonical record became `0.4788`.
- The Kolibri retry also changed MATH500 from `0.984` to `0.992` and HumanEval+ from `0.774` to `0.7682926829` under unchanged result URIs. When the retried parent was later killed, several earlier succeeded Kolibri `record.json` files were rewritten as `infra_failed`.

`_run_id()` is evaluated while constructing the batch in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py`; Iris retries replay the serialized batch. `write_record()` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py` then writes unconditionally to `{prefix}/{run_id}/record.json`.

topics.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---
[Original description](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975#issuecomment-6074693580) <!-- marin-prose-cleanup -->

🤖

## Campaign 3 follow-up: constrained SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench transfer

**TL;DR:** We completed 32 constrained merges across DARE-TIES, DARE-linear, ISO, and serial DARE-TIES → ISO. Every candidate kept at least 75% of Base scalar weights bit for bit and kept every non-weight model file byte for byte. Serial-01 had the highest observed SWE-Bench-100 + TB2.1 sum at **48.17**, compared with **37.20** for Base. DARE-linear-02 reached **46.36** while changing only **2.36%** of Base scalars and is the published checkpoint.

### Results

| Checkpoint | Method | Changed (%) | SWE-Bench-100 (%) | TB2.1 (%) | Sum | Merge time (min) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Base | Control | 0.00 | 27.27 | 9.92 | 37.20 | — |
| Specialist | Control | — | 9.09 | 15.27 | 24.36 | — |
| serial-01 | Serial DARE-TIES → ISO | 10.09 | 36.00 | 12.17 | **48.17** | 140.60 |
| dare-linear-02 | DARE-linear | 2.36 | 33.00 | 13.36 | **46.36** | 38.21 |
| dare-ties-04 | DARE-TIES | 2.50 | 34.00 | 11.74 | **45.74** | 42.34 |

The serial family had the highest mean sum, 41.72, and the best single result. Its four 12.50%-support variants averaged 45.43, while its four 25%-support variants averaged 38.00, so changing more Base parameters did not improve this family. DARE-linear averaged 39.61, DARE-TIES 38.48, and ISO 38.17. ISO-08 was ISO's best result at 44.83, but changed 23.93% and took 101.89 minutes.

The specialist control was better than Base on TB2.1 and much worse on SWE-Bench-100. The best merges recovered part of that TB2.1 advantage while preserving or improving SWE-Bench performance. None matched the specialist's 15.27 TB2.1 score, and this campaign did not evaluate any non-target benchmark.

### Protocol

Base was [`open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10/tree/153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f) at revision `153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f`. The specialist was [`laion/snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203`](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203/tree/ff664b48f4c79a81c585dbc9e082b34af3a22b4a) at revision `ff664b48f4c79a81c585dbc9e082b34af3a22b4a`.

Each candidate could change only routed-expert weight matrices. The final checkpoint could differ from original Base at no more than 25% of scalar weight positions. Tensor names, shapes, dtypes, shard layout, configuration, tokenizer, chat template, generation settings, weight index, and all other non-weight files had to match Base exactly. Every export received a full stored-weight and file-inventory readback audit against original Base, including both stages of serial merges.

We ran eight variants in each family. Variants 01–04 used a 12.50% support cap and variants 05–08 used 25.00%.

| Family | Four settings at each support cap |
| --- | --- |
| DARE-TIES | `(keep, scale)` = `(0.20, 0.10)`, `(0.20, 0.25)`, `(0.50, 0.25)`, `(0.50, 0.50)`; magnitude trim 0.20 |
| DARE-linear | The same keep/scale pairs without magnitude trimming |
| ISO | Retain 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, or 1.00 of singular-vector modes |
| Serial DARE-TIES → ISO | DARE-TIES `(keep=0.20, scale=0.25, trim=0.20)`, then the four ISO settings |

Expert support was benchmark independent. For each layer, expert IDs were sorted by SHA256 of `0:layer:expert`, selected round-robin across layers, and applied to all three expert projections. The smaller support was a prefix of the larger support.

Evaluation used Marin commit `554a4b0758448039aa26cf2502ab6eed3c637054`, release base `aaf1878ce65a1a05b386aef257b952fa7205283a`, and Harbor commit `2203bacd03d82e9d4f2a9422f0b3f7e9bb7952cc`. SWE-Bench used `DCAgent2/swebench-verified-random-100-folders` at revision `0c553bd6d05d451907afb8db31dba84759ccc993`, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, one trial per task, 32,768 input tokens, 8,192 output tokens, and a 90% scored-trial gate. TB2.1 used `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1` ref 6, Terminus-2, 89 tasks with three attempts each, 65,536 input tokens, 16,384 output tokens, and a 75% scored-trial gate.

Both evaluations used 16 concurrent trials, a 360-second setup timeout, a 1,800-second agent timeout, a 300-second verifier timeout, and at most ten retries. Each model used one shared eight-H100 inference server for its two evaluations. At most eight model groups ran concurrently.

The final three TB2.1 runs were early-sealed after they passed the authorized 75% scored-trial gate. Serial-08 sealed at 260/267 scored trials and 12.31%, dare-linear-08 at 222/267 and 9.91%, and iso-08 at 261/267 and 11.49%. Scores are mean reward over valid scored trials, with coverage reported separately.

All 32 candidates and both controls have accepted SWE-Bench-100 and TB2.1 results. All campaign jobs are terminal and zero H100s remain reserved.

### Public artifacts

- [Recipes, evaluation configs, protocol, audit summary, and complete tracker](https://gist.github.com/penfever/f93b39b8cc6dd12674e5e083f80c63d4)
- [Core merge implementation: PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974)
- [Published DARE-linear-02 checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12/tree/271c4b3c6b38e8f645c88b8938a6ccf2b2195f2a)

Raw benchmark transcripts and trial artifacts are not redistributed because the public bundle does not establish redistribution rights for them. The public files reproduce checkpoint construction and evaluation configuration, but external readers cannot independently reaggregate the reported scores from raw trials. The 32 candidates were selected and ranked on these same two target benchmarks; the point estimates do not establish statistical significance, full SWE-Bench Verified performance, or non-target capability retention.

topics.title: [analysis] Independent pre-registered forecast of the hero's final loss, with 80/95% intervals
topics.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

topics.body: Negative-step slices of sharded cache flat fields returned empty arrays because the reader requested a zero-length forward span. Read the covered span in forward order, then apply the negative stride. Reverse slices now return values across shard boundaries.

topics.title: [post-training] Transfer two Snowball experts at once: MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and weight merging
topics.body:
Follow-up to #9920 (single-expert transfer: plain SFT, RS-SFT and OPD each moved the CruxEval expert E's gain back into the Snowball student B). Design note is kept by the owner; this issue is the summary and coordination record.

**TL;DR.** Done; the single consolidated report is https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984#issuecomment-6144923850. A second expert E_2 (B fine-tuned on GLM 5.3 MMLU-Pro traces with E's recipe) reached 66.4% on its 1,606-doc MMLU-Pro subset (B 44.5%) and 64.0% on the 10,426 held-out docs (B 44.1%); its CruxEval output was 4.9 pp below B in one pass. Four ways of putting E and E_2 into B at once were compared on both domains plus GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA-D and IFEval. At the selected finals, mixed SFT-RS (step-727) is above MOPD (step-100) on the MMLU-Pro subset (+4.0 pp [+1.6, +6.3]) with the held-out difference unresolved (+0.4 [−0.5, +1.4]); MOPD is above RS on CruxEval input (+4.9 [+1.6, +8.1]) with the output difference unresolved. Both improve both domains over B; neither is a matched control for the other (unequal compute, token budgets and verifier access). Plain mixed SFT recovers less; half-strength merging scores above B in both domains with no training but below the trained arms on CruxEval output, and the full-strength task-arithmetic merge regresses badly on GSM8K and GPQA-D. Training allocations: E_2 60.6, RS 93.6, plain 122.0, MOPD 557.9 H100-h; evaluation serve allocation 1,752.6 H100-h, 894.5 of it in 31 groups that produced no record (mostly serves left running on stale endpoints). Two record-provenance defects and an evaluator-revision label error were found in review and corrected before publication; the RS demo selector used a different answer-extraction rule from the evaluator (14 of 1,400 selected demos affected), stated beside the RS results.

**Questions.**
1. Do the experts themselves collapse in the other domain after GLM SFT? (E on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-D; E_2 on CruxEval; both on GSM8K.)
2. When both experts are transferred into B at once, how much of each domain is recovered and how much of the other is lost?
3. How do MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and merging compare on that, and at what cost?

**Models.** B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5` (unchanged). E = the #9920 CruxEval expert (`…/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`; CruxEval 79.4 / 71.4 vs B 55.4 / 57.8; GPQA-D 44.8% vs B 41.9%, 198 questions × 3 repeats, no observed drop). E_2 = B + full SFT on GLM 5.3 MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe: AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer state, frozen router bias, 32 H100.

**E_2 domain and data.** MMLU-Pro (B 44.1%, GLM 5.3 85.8% under the frozen evaluator). The GLM trace collection had indexed the dataset by question text; 200 questions appear in 2–3 prompt variants, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold letter and 175 GLM grades flipped. Every captured doc was re-joined to the pinned dataset (TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec765aa7ed75c8acfea42df31fdae71f97be`) by exact question + ordered options and relabelled; B's stored per-doc labels were independently correct (5,303/12,032 = 44.07% under both label sets). Training subset: a seeded, category-proportional draw of whole question groups (every prompt variant of a picked question travels with it): 1,589 questions = 1,606 docs, 1,359 with a usable GLM trace (correct, finished, reasoning present, fits 32,768 tokens under B's template); 729,901 supervised tokens per epoch. Docs without a usable trace stay in the subset denominator untrained. The other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and scored as a probe. B on the subset 43.9%, on the remainder 44.1%; GLM 85.7% / 85.9%. Artifacts (SHA-pinned, independently verified): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`.

**E_2 gate (operational).** Paired gain over B on the subset ≥ 10 pp as a point estimate and lower 95% group-bootstrap bound ≥ 5 pp on the first pass; if the first pass lands in [8, 10) on the gain or [3, 5) on the bound, one second pass is run and the gate is re-evaluated on both passes pooled (never the better pass). GSM8K paired drop over 2 pp stops the arm. CruxEval, GPQA-D, MATH500 and the held-out score are reported, not gated.

**Frozen evaluator.** As #9920: Evalchemy `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8` (the label `c131e5ab` given here before 2026-10-13 was the unused code constant; the revision is read from each record's `eval_runtime`), vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, temperature 1.0 unseeded. MMLU-Pro runs always score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record against the canonical labels, with bootstrap intervals that resample question groups.

**Arms (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the same 3,206 prompts = 1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- MOPD from E + E_2: 4 rollouts per prompt, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (MarinSkyRL routed teachers), one teacher node each.
- Mixed SFT: one demo per prompt (E's sample 0 from the #9920 k=8 CruxEval pool; E_2's sample 0 from a new k=8 collection on the 1,606), the SFT counterpart of MOPD on the same prompts and epochs (prompt-matched, not token-matched).
- Mixed SFT-RS: first execution-correct (CruxEval) or answer-correct (MMLU-Pro) sample per prompt from the two k=8 pools; uncovered prompts stay in the denominators. Uses verifier access the other arms do not have.
- Merge B + E + E_2: #9974 tools with B as anchor and E, E_2 as donors, task arithmetic B + a·(E−B) + b·(E_2−B) over a small coefficient grid plus TIES and DARE-TIES; CPU only, no training.
- Dropped: OPD from E_2 alone and plain SFT from E_2 demos alone (the single-expert question was answered in #9920).

**Selection and reporting.** As #9920: prefer the final checkpoint when it is similar or better on every target metric (similar = paired 95% CI includes 0, an operational threshold); otherwise a second pass on the last two checkpoints and the two-pass means decide. Costs in H100-hours from Iris task durations (method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298); full-run figures labelled as such; demo generation counted once; failed-eval overhead separate. One consolidated final comment; no running log here.

**Budget (planning estimates).** E_2 ≈ 30–40 H100-h; k=8 E_2 demos on 1,606 prompts ≈ 2; MOPD ≈ 300–500 (7 nodes; set by the smoke run); mixed SFT and SFT-RS ≈ 60–120 each; merge CPU only; evaluations ≈ 150.

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-13: final report posted; selections RS step-727, plain step-803 (two-pass means), MOPD step-100; evaluator revision label corrected to ae362881; B and MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro figures restated from the pinned FineStore manifests.
- 2026-10-09: MMLU-Pro chosen as E_2's domain (GPQA-D too small to train on: 198 questions). Subset = whole question groups, ~1,600 docs; remainder held out as a probe. GLM labels repaired and verified by two agents; B labels confirmed. Arms fixed to MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merge(B,E,E_2); OPD-from-E_2 and E_2-only SFT dropped. New issue opened rather than continuing in #9920.

comments.body:
🤖 **Final report: two experts into one student (MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merging)**

**Summary.** E_2 reached 66.4% on the MMLU-Pro subset used for its fine-tuning (B 44.5%) and 64.0% on the remaining docs (B 44.1%). Its CruxEval output score was 4.9 percentage points below B in one pass. Its IFEval instruction-strict point estimate was also below B (80.2% versus 81.1%), with an interval spanning zero; the other reported probe point estimates were above B. At the selected finals, mixed SFT-RS step-727 exceeds MOPD step-100 on the MMLU-Pro subset by 4.0 pp [1.6, 6.3]; the held-out difference is unresolved (+0.4 [−0.5, 1.4]). MOPD exceeds RS on CruxEval input by 4.9 pp [1.6, 8.1]; the output difference is unresolved. RS-727 and MOPD-100 are the selected finals of their arms (RS-727 similar to 546, MOPD-100 similar to 50 on every target). They use unequal compute, token budgets and verifier access. Plain-SFT step-803 was selected on two-pass means. The RS arm's demo selector used a different answer-extraction rule from the evaluator (quantified under Caveats). Weight merging at half strength scores above B in both domains with no training (CruxEval input 76.5, output 67.6; MMLU-Pro subset 63.2), below the trained arms on CruxEval output; the full-strength task-arithmetic merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs. Training-gang allocations: RS-SFT 93.6 H100-h, MOPD 557.9 (2 epochs, 7 nodes; plus 28.3 of export-only jobs). Evaluation serve allocation across the 82 eval groups: 1,752.6 H100-h, of which 894.5 in 31 groups with no successful eval child (details under Costs).

**Setup (unchanged from #9920 except where stated).** B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`. E = #9920's CruxEval expert (step-272). E_2 = B + full SFT on GLM 5.3 MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe (AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer, frozen router bias, 32 H100), 1,359 usable traces over a seeded category-proportional draw of whole question-text groups (1,589 questions = 1,606 docs); the other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and used as an additional probe (prior exposure of either split during B's own training is not ruled out; both primary targets are test-exposed). Labels: the GLM collection had keyed the dataset by question text, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold; every doc was re-joined to TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec76` by exact question + ordered options (artifacts and SHA-256 at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`, independently verified against the pinned source and captured prompts; verification artifact `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/task162-candidate-verification-v4/`). Transfer arms start from B with matched AdamW hyperparameters (LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, gradient clip 1.0) and frozen router bias, implemented in Levanter for SFT and Megatron for MOPD. The shared evaluation universe has 3,206 prompts (1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro). Plain SFT trains four epochs on 3,206 sample-zero demonstrations; RS-SFT trains four epochs on 2,903 covered prompts. MOPD runs two epochs with four rollouts per sampled prompt and domain-routed teachers (100 optimizer updates of 64 prompts; 50 per epoch). These budgets are not token- or compute-matched. MOPD = MarinSkyRL on-policy distillation with two pinned teachers, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (sampled reverse KL, 4 rollouts per prompt, 1:1 route mix). Mixed SFT = one demo per prompt (E's and E_2's sample 0 from k=8 pools). Mixed SFT-RS = the first sample per prompt in index order that is execution-correct (CruxEval) or accepted by the implemented answer selector (MMLU-Pro) from the same k=8 pools (1,503 + 1,400 covered prompts; uncovered prompts stay in every denominator). Merges = #9974 tools, B anchor, E and E_2 donors: task arithmetic at a = b = 0.5 and a = b = 1.0, and TIES (density 0.5, a = b = 1.0); CPU only.

**Frozen evaluator.** Evalchemy `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8` (recorded in every record's `eval_runtime`; the `c131e5ab` label in earlier text was an unused code constant and has been corrected in #9920), vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, unseeded sampling at temperature 1.0. MMLU-Pro runs score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record's active FineStore snapshot against the canonical gold; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro (subset 1,589, held-out 10,212) and problems within each CruxEval direction (800), conditional on the observed sampled completions; they do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability. At ae362881, MMLU-Pro extraction uses final content when available, falls back to reasoning for REASONING_ONLY responses, and returns no answer for truncated reasoning-only responses; it applies `final_response_text`, then the three answer-letter regexes, and uppercases the result. Exact replay reproduced native predictions on all 12,032 rows of each of B-220c, E_2-254, RS-727 and MOPD-100. The broader matrix has uniform runtime-revision metadata; it was not replayed in full. The stored normalized output is not always the scorer input (the scorer saw the parser-split final content), so re-grading must start from the native completions. All comparisons are paired on the same docs.

**Results, MMLU-Pro** (single pass per checkpoint; subset % / held-out % / all %; Δ = paired vs B on the subset, pp with 95% group bootstrap; B 44.46 / 44.05 / 44.11; E 60.34 / 59.76 / 59.84; E_2 66.44 / 63.97 / 64.30).

| MOPD step-50 | 65.01 | 65.57 | 65.49 | +20.6 [+17.9, +23.1] |

**Results, CruxEval and probes** (CruxEval input / output pass@1 of 800 each; GSM8K flexible; single pass unless stated).

**Paired deltas (pp, 95% bootstrap).** All plain-803-versus-other-model intervals below use its pass 1; both passes are shown in the tables, and selection uses their mean. CruxEval vs B (in / out): MOPD-100 +26.75 [+23.0, +30.5] / +18.6 [+15.0, +22.25]; RS-727 +21.9 [+17.9, +25.75] / +19.5 [+15.75, +23.1]; plain-803 +20.0 [+16.0, +24.0] / +13.75 [+9.9, +17.5]; TA-0.5 +21.1 / +9.9; TIES +17.4 / +10.4. The following CruxEval-versus-E deltas use E's first CruxEval pass (635/800 input, 562/800 output), not the two-pass E mean displayed in the table; plain-803 deltas here use its first pass, and both plain passes are reported together for selection. CruxEval vs E: MOPD-100 +2.75 [−0.5, +5.9] / +6.1 [+2.9, +9.4]; RS-727 −2.1 [−5.6, +1.5] / +7.0 [+3.75, +10.4]; plain-803 −4.0 [−7.75, −0.4] / +1.25 [−2.0, +4.6]; TA-0.5 −2.9 / −2.6; TIES −6.6 / −2.1. MMLU-Pro vs E_2 (subset / held-out): MOPD-100 −2.2 [−4.5, +0.1] / +0.4 [−0.5, +1.3]; RS-727 +1.7 [−0.5, +4.2] / +0.8 [−0.2, +1.8]. Cross-arm (selected finals): RS-727 − MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro +4.0 [+1.6, +6.3] / +0.4 [−0.5, +1.4]; CruxEval −4.9 [−8.1, −1.6] / +0.9 [−2.1, +3.75]. RS-727 − plain-803 MMLU-Pro +5.8 [+3.5, +8.2] / +1.9 [+1.0, +2.9]. Experts across domains: E on MMLU-Pro +15.9 [+13.5, +18.3] over B on the subset without training on it; E_2 on CruxEval −0.9 / −4.9 vs B. IFEval, official instruction-level strict (sum of correct instructions over 834 instructions, prompt-resampling bootstrap): E − B −2.2 [−4.7, +0.2]; E_2 − B −0.8 [−3.2, +1.4]; RS-727 − B −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24] (loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 − B −1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] (loose +0.24 [−2.02, +2.48]); RS-727 − E −0.60 [−3.05, +1.93]; MOPD-100 − E +1.08 [−1.42, +3.57]; RS-727 − MOPD-100 −1.68 [−4.21, +0.95]. GPQA-D (198 questions × 3 repeats, per-question means, question bootstrap): RS-727 − B +15.7 [+10.4, +21.0]; MOPD-100 − B +5.6 [+0.7, +10.4]; RS-727 − MOPD-100 +10.1 [+5.7, +14.5]; RS-727 − E_2 +9.9 [+5.4, +14.5].

**Selection (frozen rule: final checkpoint unless a target metric is lower with the interval excluding 0; then a second pass on the last two and the two-pass means decide; the held-out probe is never an input).** Mixed SFT-RS: step-727 vs 546 similar on MMLU-Pro subset (+1.0 [−1.25, +3.3]) and CruxEval (−1.5 [−5.0, +1.9] / +1.25 [−1.9, +4.4]) → step-727 selected. Mixed SFT: step-803 vs 603 was lower on CruxEval input in pass 1 (−3.9 [−7.5, −0.25]) → second pass on both. On per-item two-pass means (paired, bootstrap over problems / question groups), 803 − 603 = CruxEval input −2.25 [−4.94, +0.38], output −0.12 [−2.56, +2.50], MMLU-Pro subset +1.56 [−0.09, +3.19] (held-out +1.00 [+0.33, +1.63], not a selection input): similar on every target → step-803 selected. The pass-to-pass swings at fixed weights (603 CruxEval input 79.25 → 75.4; 803 MMLU-Pro subset 62.39 → 61.71) are the run-to-run measurements this experiment has; pass-1 intervals do not include them. MOPD: step-50 has two valid CruxEval records, 641/585 from the first group (`20261011-035349`, whose MMLU-Pro and GSM8K evals failed) and 644/608 from the retry group (`20261013-023108`, which produced all three records); no rule fixed before scoring chose between them, and the retry record was used as the selection input because its group is the one that completed. Step-100 vs step-50 (paired, single pass each, retry record): MMLU-Pro subset −0.81 [−2.99, +1.55], CruxEval +1.62 [−1.50, +4.75] / +0.38 [−2.62, +3.38] → similar on every target → step-100 selected; the held-out probe favours step-50 by 1.2 pp [−2.08, −0.36], reported as context. Sensitivity with both step-50 CruxEval passes (step-100 single pass vs the per-problem two-pass mean of step-50, 80.31 / 74.56): +1.81 [−0.94, +4.50] / +1.81 [−1.00, +4.56]; same decision. Merges: single artifacts, no selection.

**Reading the result.** (1) At RS-727 and MOPD-100, both domains improve over B. Relative to the specialists, MOPD's MMLU-Pro subset difference from E_2 is −2.24 pp [−4.47, +0.06], while RS's is +1.74 pp with an interval spanning zero. Intervals spanning zero do not establish preservation or equivalence. Both checkpoints have higher CruxEval output scores than E's first pass; their input differences from E are unresolved. Paired changes versus B on each split: MOPD-100 +19.7 pp on the subset and +20.3 on the held-out docs; RS-727 +23.7 and +20.7. (2) RS-SFT and MOPD differ by domain: RS higher on the MMLU-Pro subset, MOPD higher on CruxEval input, output unresolved. RS-SFT had ground-truth verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and an unequal token budget; MOPD had on-policy samples scored by the teachers. Neither is a matched control for the other. (3) Plain mixed SFT recovers less than either (MMLU-Pro −5.8 pp vs RS; CruxEval below E on input). (4) Merging recovers CruxEval input (76.5 at a = b = 0.5) and most of MMLU-Pro (63.2) with no training, but its CruxEval output (67.6) is 2.6 pp below E's first pass (70.25), 3.8 below E's two-pass mean (71.4), 8.8 below MOPD-100 (76.4), 9.65 below RS-727 (77.25) and 3.9 below plain-803's first pass (71.5); TIES output (68.1) sits 0.5 pp above TA-0.5 on each of those comparisons; at full strength (a = b = 1.0) the merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs (median 85–95k characters), so it was withheld from the rest of the matrix. (5) Probes on the two finals (single pass each; 0 infrastructure-error rows; MATH500 median output 2,496 and 1,525 characters): RS-727 MATH500 92.4, GPQA-D 57.6, IFEval instruction-strict 78.3 (below B with the interval excluding 0: −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24]; loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 MATH500 90.0, GPQA-D 47.5, IFEval 80.0 (−1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] vs B). RS-727's GPQA-D score is above every other model in this matrix (B 41.9, E 44.8, E_2 47.6, MOPD-100 47.5, merges 47.1–47.3); it is one evaluation with three generations for each of 198 questions and is reported with its paired interval, not interpreted.

**Caveats.** One pass per checkpoint except the explicitly reported repeats; plain 603/803 selection uses per-item two-pass means. Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons and checkpoint selection; additional-probe findings are exploratory. Targets are 800 problems per CruxEval direction and 1,606 docs; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro and problems within each CruxEval direction, conditional on the observed sampled completions, and do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability (E's two CruxEval passes differed by 0.1 / 2.25 pp in #9920). The MMLU-Pro subset was the fine-tuning set for E_2 and the training prompt set for every arm; the 10,426 held-out docs are an additional probe, reported and never used for selection. RS demo selector mismatch: the k=8 demo grader implemented the older first-match-anywhere extractor on the whole text, while the evaluator grades the final answer after the think block; under the evaluator's rule 14 of the 1,400 selected RS MMLU-Pro demos (1.0%) are wrong, 15 more prompts would have been covered and 1 lost, and 45 prompts would have used a different sample. The RS arm is reported as trained; no corrected run was made. Record provenance: two records (B MMLU-Pro and MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro) had a retried eval attempt that left a second full sample stream; all numbers here come from each record's pinned active FineStore manifest (HEAD), with the native writer taken from the active source-blob provenance (normalized sample rows can carry null correctness); superseded attempts are kept as overhead and evidence, not as independent repeats (an earlier reading of the first stream gave B 43.90 and MOPD-100 65.32 on the subset and has been superseded). Three merge MATH500 records from 2026-10-10 are invalid (Evalchemy `AgentTimeoutError` in 500/500, 455/500 and 300/500 rows) and were rerun for TA-0.5 and TIES; TA-1.0 was not rerun.

**Costs (H100-hours = GPUs × Iris task or attempt duration; method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298; every figure labelled by what it includes).** Training-gang allocations (image pull, load, steps, in-gang checkpoint/HF export and teardown; queue time excluded): E_2 60.6 (3 epochs, 32 H100). Mixed SFT-RS 93.57 (728 updates, 32 H100). Mixed SFT 107.83, plus 14.21 for a first attempt evicted by Kueue after 16 updates and relaunched from B. MOPD 557.9 for the 2-epoch run (100 optimizer updates, 7 × H100x8; the launch plan said ≈102, the sampler yielded 50 full windows per epoch; the W&B run `skyrl/snowball-mopd2-cruxeval-mmlupro-2ep` logged 99 steps and is marked `crashed`; coordinator logs record 100 updates and the terminal export at global_step 100 succeeded), plus 28.3 in two separate export-only jobs (step-50 13.8, step-100 14.5), which the SFT figures include in-gang; allocation to the step-50 checkpoint ≈ 317 and to step-100 ≈ 531 from timestamps (full run, not pro-rated). E_2 k=8 demo pool 8.91 (counted once, shared by both SFT arms; #9920's CruxEval pool is reused and its cost stays in #9920). Merges: CPU only (33, 28 and 68 min). Excluded from every total: GLM trace generation, E's construction (#9920), CPU preparation and audit jobs, the MOPD smoke run (≈60.6, reported in the design ledger). Evaluation serve allocation (serve attempt `started_at`→`finished_at` × 8 H100; queue time and CPU eval tasks excluded; two sweeps, 2026-10-13 05:20 and 11:40 UTC, 82 groups): 1,752.6 H100-h. topics.title: [eval] Preserve completed evaluation results on Iris retries
topics.body:
Iris retries now reuse an existing successful record before starting model serving. Conditional record publication preserves the first success when a retry later fails or concurrent attempts race. The Evalchemy child reads a FineStore completion marker and runs without a local output directory. This covers the record-to-StepSpec success gap described in #9813.

This draft cannot merge until marin-community/evalchemy publishes FineStore-backed request resume and completion markers, then Marin updates its Evalchemy pin. topics.body:
Add a preflight item to the hero cutover checklist: a one-rack run of the deploy commit restores the handoff and trains through a dropless eval and the steps after it. The 200-step trial usually ends before the new run's first eval, so a cutover can go live without ever switching between its eval and train executables, and that switch has failed before (#8861).

Also note that the public hero report starts each phase's curves at the run's `report_phase_start` config value. The 2026-10-09 handoff to `hero-mfu30-step231k` showed its whole inherited history until the value was set.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the Taskforge pipeline skeleton
topics.body:
This draft is kept as the reference implementation of Taskforge and as the surface for its line-by-line review. A minimal PR cut from main supersedes it for merge: it adds the real GLM client through Ortet and an experiment that prompts GLM with a catalog.json entry to write a program, runs the program in Shellbox and saves the TaskSpec the program emits. The follow-ups are cut from this draft, roughly one per stage: proposal, triage, builder author and builder runtime, validate, review, the stage coordinator, the ledger if it is still needed, and Zephyr. The inline review comments on this draft are their to-do list, and each comment names the PR that fixes it. The branch is not rewritten, so the comments stay anchored to 8dbf74d5.

The draft adds lib/taskforge, the task-generation library, and experiments/post_training/capability_driven_envs, which runs it over the capability catalog with scripted models and in-process ShellSim.

A build program is a DAG of pure steps with one sink. Steps declare their inputs, and a step's cache key is its own source plus the digests of its inputs, so editing one step reruns only it and the steps downstream of it. The proposal is a declarable input; steps that do not read it keep their cache across proposal changes. One runner sequences the steps and records them. The library ships no concrete steps.

Taskforge is a state machine over stages: triage, author, build, validate, review and done, with the edges as a transition table and an item's state as a pure fold over its JSONL event log. The caller passes the stage functions as a typed bundle, so the type checker validates the composition; the loop coordinates them, records one event per stage and resumes an interrupted item from its log. Run inputs are pinned to the run root: the policy, including the session limits validation imposes on every trial, is written once, and a relaunch with a different policy or a changed idea record is refused. The modify edge from review back to the author is in the table and never taken here.

Proposals and build call models through one surface, ModelClient, and every call is recorded with its item, round and step. Validation runs the solver through RolloutEngine: a ModelFactory builds one rollout model per trial from the policy's sampling. Triage accepts every proposal, validation lowers the task onto ShellSim and runs k solver trials, and review decides from the band rules. A grading infrastructure error retries the trial; it does not reject the task.

Taskforge is a root-lock workspace member with a dedicated CI suite, as RolloutEngine is. The draft has no GLM client (only the ModelClient protocol and NoModel), no reference step SDK, no triage repair, no controls or adversary trials, and no queue or Docker machines.

topics.title: [zephyr] Add opt-in intra-shard map execution
topics.body:
Add `ZephyrContext(intra_shard_execution=IntraShardExecution.AUTO)` to execute row maps, filters, selections, and flat maps within an existing shard across workers. Callbacks must not depend on per-shard mutable state. The default is `OFF`. The planner adds `Split → Map → Concat`, dividing Parquet sources into row ranges when there are fewer source shards than `max_workers`; later stages split at existing chunk boundaries. Ordered concatenation restores original shard IDs, row order, and output filenames before shard-level operations and writes.

Maps immediately preceding an explicit-schema Parquet sink produce Parquet fragments for an Arrow-batch final writer. Other map intermediates use pickle chunks. Concatenation avoids a key shuffle, but final assembly still decodes and re-encodes Parquet. Batch-mode sources retain their batch boundaries, and `map_shard` callbacks remain indivisible.

Fixed local samples from TaskTrove dataset revision `02923004846e4e73862c20962f823a6d05100e7a`, each with one row group, used [conversion code at ee20e03517](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ee20e03517/experiments/post_training/task_curation) through Zephyr's `SubprocessRunner`. All columns use `AUTO`; one worker retains fused execution. Single-run wall times on a shared Ryzen 7 3800X include startup, intermediate I/O, final write, and shutdown:

| Sample | Rows | 1 worker | 2 workers | 4 workers |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Structured outputs | 10,000 | 79.81s | 58.77s | 34.93s |
| SWE-smith | 2,000 | 33.93s | 31.09s | 21.83s |
| SWE-rebench | 2,000 | 19.90s | 23.33s | 20.37s |
| TACO | 2,000 | 68.80s | 36.74s | 24.44s |

All runs matched the one-worker baseline's complete record content, rejection outcomes, source order, and single output file layout. Four-worker final Parquet read/write took 3.47–9.75s; SWE-rebench showed no end-to-end improvement. Peak summed process-tree RSS ranged from 2.25 to 3.00 GiB at four workers. Workers still read overlapping row groups in full, so row offsets increase read work and memory. Host load varied during these runs; they are not stable throughput estimates.
